p.seg: A disciple said:
"Then what is there to worry about?"
The Master said:
"It is not for you to know.
You, my followers, all take part in the morning deliberations on governance,
but now you speak of government without touching on transformation;
this means there is no ritual in All Under Heaven.
You speak of music without touching on refinement;
this means there is no joy in All Under Heaven.
You speak of literature without touching on principle;
this means there is no culture in All Under Heaven.
From where can the royal way arise?
This is why I worry."
The disciples withdrew. The Master took up the qín and played the "Dàng" section;
the disciples all soaked their lapels with tears.
The Master said:
"Some act at ease,
some act for profit,
some act out of fear;
but when the task is accomplished,
it is one.
Measured by virtue, it is distant."
Jiǎ Qióng, reciting the *Shū* to the "Mandate of Huán Róng,"
said:
"How vast! How bright this enterprise.
Heaven truly observes you;
can you not end it with yielding and deference?"
Fán Shīxuán was about to compose the "Beǐ Qí Record,"
and told the Master;
the Master said:
"Do not compose it carelessly."
Yuè Gōng sent the Master the "*Classic of Food*," but the Master did not accept it.
He said:
"Soup of pigweed with bits of dried food inside—
there is no use for it."
He responded with the "Wine Proclamation" and the Three Virtues of the "Great Plan."
The Master said:
"The petty person is not stirred nor spurred,
and is not encouraged when not seeing profit."
Jìng Jūnliàng asked about disgrace.
The Master said:
"If words are not accurate,
and conduct is not cautious,
that is disgrace."
The Master said:
"When transformation reaches nine changes,
will not the kingly way then be bright?
Thus, when music reaches nine changes,
the pure vital energy is abundant."
Péi Xī said:
"What does this mean?"
The Master said:
"Music
is what expresses the fulfillment of forms.
Nothing surpasses the form in expressing fulfillment,
and it disperses into sound;
from the beginning to the end of royal transformation, it can be seen.
Therefore, when the "Sháo" is accomplished,
the kindness of the Yú clan extends even to plants and animals;
the nests of crows and magpies
can be seen by looking down,
so why should the phoenix conceal itself?"
The Master said:
"The expenditures for fèngshàn sacrifices
are not in accord with antiquity,
but merely to boast before All Under Heaven;
is this not the extravagant heart of Qín and Hàn?"
The Master said:
"Those who easily feel joy must often experience sorrow;
those who give lightly are surely fond of taking away."
The Master said:
"A country with no pardons—
its punishments will surely be just.
A country with many levies—
its wealth must be diminished."
The Master said:
"The honest are always happy and ask nothing;
the greedy are always worried and never feel they have enough."
The Master said:
"If Dù Rúhuì were to meet a true king,
would he not be, for the ten thousand people, like Heaven itself?"
Dǒng Cháng, Fáng Yuánlíng, and Jiǎ Qióng asked:
"What do you mean?"
The Master said:
"In spring things are born,
in summer they grow,
in autumn they mature,
in winter they are gathered in.
The father is able to be a father,
the son is able to be a son,
the ruler is able to be a ruler,
the minister is able to be a minister,
all types are rightly ordered."
"What the people use every day without knowing—
this is Dù's office.
Would you not call it like Heaven itself?
I have observed this for long;
my sight is dazzled,
my spirit startled.
As for those who recognize fate and timing,
their worry of not meeting a true lord is because of this!"
Shū Tián said:
"Shùn, in a single year, made offerings at the Five Peaks;
the state was not impoverished and the people were not wearied.
How so?"
The Master said:
"There is no other reason—
it was the Way.
There were few guards and the exactions were few."
The Master said:
"When a royal state has ballads,
is the Son of Heaven equal to the feudal lords?
Who takes precedence?
It is the fault of Yōu Wáng.
Thus it began with the "Millet Departure,"
and at that the elegant way ceased."
The Master said:
"If the Five Phases do not oppose each other,
then the king can regulate rites;
if the Four Spirits are domesticated,
then the king can create music."
Zǐ Yóu visited the temple of Kǒngzǐ.
On coming out, he sang:
"How great it is!
The ruler is ruler, the minister is minister,
the father is father, the son is son,
the elder brother is elder brother, the younger brother is younger brother,
the husband is husband, the wife is wife!
This is the achievement of the Master;
does it not join virtue with the Supreme Ultimate,
and accompany the divine way?"
Wáng Xiàoyì said:
"Is the Master's Way
really so little?"
The Master said:
"Have you not recited the "White Jade" three times?
Heaven and earth give birth to me,
but cannot nurture me;
my parents nurture me,
but cannot complete me;
the one who completes me is the Master.
The Way surpasses even heaven, earth, and parents,
and is communicated through the Master;
I receive a boundless favor.
How could you disrupt proper human relationships?
Xiàoyì bowed twice in thanks,
and never again dared to criticize or praise."
Wéi Dǐng requested an audience.
The Master received him three times yet said nothing,
remaining earnest, as if not enough.
When Dǐng left, he said to the disciples:
"If the Master attains his vision at court,
there would be a transformation without words
and a severity without killing."
Yáng Sù spoke to the Master, saying:
"The Son of Heaven is seeking those skilled in defending the border.
I have heard that only the worthy recognize the worthy.
May I ask the Master."
The Master said:
"Yáng Hù and Lù Xùn
were humane men;
they could be so employed."
Sù said:
"But they are dead.
How can they be used again?"
The Master said:
"If you, sir, can perform what Yáng and Lù did, then it is possible;
if you cannot,
what use is there in seeking widely?
If communication is heard:
those nearby rejoice,
those far away come;
and conflicts can be settled at the wine-table.
Why must one go to the very border?"
In the house of the Master,
the Six Classics are fully provided;
court attire and sacrificial vessels need not be borrowed.
He said:
“The Three Bonds and Five Constants
can arise of themselves.”
The Master said:
“Those who idly consume without endeavor—
such fill the world;
how then can the Kingly Way flourish?”
The Master said:
“He who rules the Seven Regulations—
such a person is ready for war.”
Dǒng Cháng having died,
the Master wept outside the bedchamber door
and bowed to receive condolence.
Péi Xī asked, saying:
“Wèi Jiè said that if one fails to measure up,
one may forgive with feeling;
if one offends unintentionally,
one may excuse by reason.
What do you think?”
The Master said:
“How magnanimous!”
He asked:
“Is this benevolence?”
The Master said:
“I do not know.”
Ruǎn Sìzōng, when speaking with others,
would always reach for the profound and remote;
he never praised or disparaged others’ character.
What do you think?”
The Master said:
“How cautious!”
He asked:
“Is this benevolence?”
The Master said:
“I do not know.”
The Master said:
“How forgiving Líng Jìng is!
He treats the orphans of others as if they were his own.”
The Master said:
“A benevolent one—
I have not been able to meet;
if I could meet a wise one,
that would suffice.
A wise one—
I have not been able to meet;
if I could meet a just one,
that would suffice.
If even that cannot be found,
then must it be one who is firm and unyielding?
The firm delight in decisiveness;
the unyielding differ from the common.”
Xuē Shōu asked about the essentials of utmost virtue.
The Master said:
“Utmost virtue
—is it not the very root of the Way?
The essential way
—is it not the very practice of virtue?
Does not the Book of Rites say:
‘Utmost virtue is the root of the Way’?
Does not the Book of Changes say:
‘Manifest the Way, spiritual virtue is practiced’?”
The Master said:
“Vast and marvelous is the numinous!
That from which all proceeds.
Profound indeed, the Book of Changes!
Does it not know the doings of the numinous?”
The Master said:
“I have yet to see one who delights in righteousness as he delights in gain.”
The Master ascended the city of Yúnzhōng,
and gazed toward the pass of Lóngmén.
He said:
“Magnificent is the solidity of the mountains and rivers!”
Jiǎ Qióng said:
“Magnificent it is indeed;
but what can be added to it?”
The Master said:
“Guard it with the Way.”
Coming down, he spent the night at the Temple of Yǔ;
reading the inscription atop the stele, it said:
“Composed by the former lord, Xiàn Gōng.”
The writing is dignified and fluent.
The Master saw Liú Xiàobiāo’s ‘On Severing Relations’,
and said:
“How regrettable,
praising Rèn Gōng only to denigrate him.
Rèn Gōng, in this case, cannot be said to know people.”
He saw ‘On Debating Fate’,
and said:
“The Way among men is lost.”
The Master said:
“Had Zhūgě Liàng not died,
would not rites and music have flourished?”
The Master read ‘On Yuè Yì’,
and said:
“How benevolent was Yuè Yì!
He excelled at preserving his talents.
How wise was Tàichū!
He excelled at expressing his inner richness.”
The Master read ‘On the Nonexistence of Ghosts’
and said:
“If we do not yet know people,
how can we know ghosts?”
The Master said:
“The round is active;
the square is still.
Do you not see the mind of Heaven and Earth?”
The Master said:
“The wise rejoice—
is this due to the purpose of preserving things?
The benevolent live long—
is this due to the act of self-forgetfulness?”
The Master said:
“Yì is pure and dignified;
Jìng is gracious and decisive;
Wēi is gentle and broad;
Shōu is open and solemn;
Qióng is clear and resolute;
Yān is sincere and firm;
Xuánlíng is focused and discreet;
Zhēng is upright and accomplished;
Dàyǎ is deep and grand;
Shūdá is simple and correct.
If these met their proper time,
they would not fall short of ministers and counsellors;
but as for rites and music, they are not yet complete.”
Someone asked:
“What kind of person was Dǒng Cháng?”
The Master said:
“In action he was discerning;
in stillness, profound.
Is he not of the school of the Yán family?”
Shū Tián said:
“When Shān Tāo served as Minister of Personnel,
he selected the worthy and advanced the good;
but in his time none recognized him.
After his death,
the Son of Heaven presented his memorials before the court;
only then did they know all the talents had been advanced by Tāo.
What do you think?”
The Master said:
“How subtle!”
He asked:
“Is this benevolence?”
The Master said:
“I do not know.”
Lǐ Mì met the Master to discuss warfare.
The Master said:
“If it be based on ritual, trust, benevolence, and righteousness,
then I will discuss it;
if it be based in isolation, cunning, deception, and force,
I will not participate.”
Lǐ Bóyào met the Master to discuss poetry.
The Master did not respond.
Bóyào withdrew and said to Xuē Shōu:
“My discourse covers Chén and Liú above,
and recounts Shěn and Xiè below;
analyzing the four tones and eight defects,
contrasting hard and soft, clear and turbid,
each in proper order;
the sound is like that of xūn and chí.
Yet the Master did not reply to me—
does this mean he has not attained understanding?”
Xuē Shōu said:
“I have heard Master’s discourse on the Shī:
above, it clarifies the Three Bonds,
below, it comprehends the Five Constants.
Thus it examines existence and extinction,
distinguishes gain and loss.
Therefore, the petty man sings them to present his customs,
the gentleman composes them to show his will,
the sage selects them to observe their transformations.
Now, you busy yourself, careening along in the minor currents;
this is what pains Master most.
If he does not answer, there is a reason.”
The Master said:
“As for learning,
is broad recitation enough?
One must be connected with the Way.
As for writing,
is it permissible to compose carelessly?
One must fulfill what is right.”
Inner Historian Xuē Gōng met the Master at Cháng’ān;
afterwards, he said to Xuē Shōu:
“The Hé-tú and the Luò-shū
are all here.
Go and serve him;
you will not go astray.”
The Master said:
“A scholar who wears fine clothes and eats delicacies yet delights in the Way—
such a one I have not yet seen.”
The Master said to Wèi Zhēng:
“You and Níng are both upright men under Heaven.
Zhēng is unbending;
Níng is towering.
If both walked among their times,
whether they would be employed or set aside is uncertain.”
The Master said to Lǐ Jìng:
“If Níng could find a place in this age,
then the royal law would not be shaken.”
Lǐ Jìng asked:
“What of making intelligence one's responsibility?”
The Master said:
“To take benevolence as one’s charge.
A petty man shoulders intelligence but abandons benevolence; such is a villain.
A gentleman shoulders intelligence but abandons benevolence; such is a sower of disorder.”
Xuē Shōu asked what sort of man Zhòngcháng Zǐguāng was.
The Master said:
“A man of Heaven.”
Shōu asked:
“What is a man of Heaven?”
The Master said:
“How minute, how small:
thus is he joined to man.
Vast, how great:
he alone can fulfill his destiny from Heaven.”
Jiǎ Qióng asked about the Way of the gentleman.
The Master said:
“Must it not begin with forbearance?”
He asked:
“May I ask for an explanation of forbearance?”
The Master said:
“As a son, take your father’s heart as your own;
as a younger brother, take your elder brother’s heart as your own.
Extend this to the world,
and it will suffice.”
The Master said:
“The learning of the gentleman advances along the Way;
the learning of the petty man advances toward profit.”
When the Chǔ rebellion arose,
the Master was summoned by an envoy,
but he did not go.
He said to the envoy:
“Convey my apologies to the Duke of Chǔ.
When the world is collapsing into chaos,
it cannot be restored without the blood and sincerity of rulers and nobles.
If the Way is not upheld,
do not seek calamity before its time.”
Lǐ Mì asked about Wáng Bà’s strategy.
The Master said:
“He would not trade the lives of a single person for all-under-heaven.”
When Lǐ Mì left,
the Master said to Jiǎ Qióng:
“The one who will bring disorder to the world is surely this man.
He takes joy in disaster and harbors thoughts of calamity,
loves strength and seeks victory—
the spirits will not side with such a one.”
At home, the Master,
even toward children, was always familiar and kindly.
When he directed people,
even toward servants and boys, he was always dignified.
The Master said:
“I have not seen anyone who truly understands fate.”
The Master said:
“Do not simply pursue profit,
do not shun harm,
do not force friendships,
do not break off ties lightly—
only one who follows the Way can do this.”
The Master personally plowed the fields.
Someone asked:
“Isn’t this laborious?”
The Master said:
“If even one man does not till,
someone may suffer hunger.
Moreover, this is the role of a common person.
Those who abandon their appointed tasks,
their guilt cannot escape Heaven and Earth—
how can I escape?”
The Master harvested millet for the threshing floor;
the yield was never more than a few shí [a unit],
and was used for sacrificial rites, marriages, and guests’ wine only;
once the rites were accomplished, he ceased.
In the Master’s household,
wine never ran dry.
Xuē Fāngshì asked about burial.
The Master said:
“The poor fold the hands and feet;
the wealthy provide a coffin and outer shell.
The size of the burial mounds should not be excessive;
they must not take up good fields.
In antiquity, the dead did not harm the living,
and excessive rites were not considered proper.”
Chén Shūdá asked about the Way of serving spirits and deities.
The Master said:
“Be respectful, but keep your distance.”
He asked about sacrificial rites.
The Master said:
“Why speak of sacrifice alone?
There is also veneration,
there is sacrifice,
there is offering.
These three are different;
in ancient times, the sages employed them to connect with the profound workings of Heaven, Earth, and Man.
Comprehend the explanations of these three,
and nothing will be beyond your grasp.”
Shūdá lowered his head.
The Master said:
“Wáng Měng had the three virtues of a gentleman:
he was cautious in serving his superiors,
gentle in associating with inferiors,
and decisive when presiding over affairs.”
Someone asked about Sū Chuò.
The Master said:
“He is a remarkable man.”
He asked:
“How is his Way?”
The Master said:
“If practiced in troubled times, it can strengthen the state;
if practiced in peace, it brings disorder.”
He asked about Niú Hóng.
The Master said:
“A man of substance.”
The Master inspected the fields;
Wèi Zhēng, Dù Yān, and Dǒng Cháng arrived.
The Master said:
“Let each state his aspiration!”
Zhēng said:
“May I serve an enlightened ruler:
when advancing, strive to offer utmost loyalty;
when withdrawing, strive to make up for faults.”
Yān said:
“May I uphold the law of an enlightened ruler,
so that under Heaven there are no wronged men.”
Cháng said:
“May the Way of the sages operate in our time;
then I need not be concerned with office or retirement.”
The Master said:
“Great indeed! I am in accord with Cháng.”
The Master was at Cháng’ān.
He said:
“Let us return!
As for those who take pleasure in the unusual and rush into advancement—
they act without consideration,
from them, there is nothing to be gained.”
The Master was in Jiàng,
and Chéng Yuán came because of Xuē Shōu.
The Master spoke with him on the Six Classics.
After leaving, Yuán said to Shōu:
"The Master upholds the everlasting order,
and brings alignment to the imperial center.
Without the Master,
I would have lost the Way and ended up on a side path."
The Master said:
"There are those who strive for reputation,
but I do not do so."
Shū Tián said:
"The teaching of Wénzhōngzǐ flourished,
perhaps at the end of the Suí dynasty,
when the royal house was yet unestablished?
Of those whose cause was failing,
I grieve that they were not employed;
of those whose cause was rising,
I regret that he could not meet them.
Was his intent diligent,
his words attested,
his actions taken with the common people at heart?"
Wénzhōngzǐ said:
"The two Emperors and three Kings
—I could not meet them,
so apart from the two Hàn dynasties, where should I turn?
How great was the ruler of the Seven Institutions!
Did he unite the world through benevolence, righteousness, impartiality, and forgiveness?
Officials were few,
punishments clear,
the gentlemen delighted in the Way,
the petty men cherished their lives.
For four hundred years,
there were no divided intentions under Heaven;
was there something that gathered people's hearts together?
To end with rites and music
—this was the achievement of the three Kings."
The Master said:
"The royal Way has been in disarray for long;
can rites and music remain uncorrected?
The great principles have grown wild indeed;
can the Shī and Shū be left without continuation?"
The Master said:
"The Way of Táng and Yú was grand precisely because it was direct,
so it ended in yielding and deference.
Surely, when a sage inherits it,
need there be fixed laws?
That Way is exceedingly broad,
and cannot be confined by later generations.
The Way of Xià and Shāng was direct through simplicity,
so it ended in banishment and usurpation.
Surely, when a sage supports it,
need it lie with me?
That Way is also vast,
and cannot be prescribed by subordinates.
If there were one to employ me,
would I not do as Zhōu Gōng once did?"
The Master was at leisure,
with Dǒng Cháng and Dòu Wēi attending.
The Master said:
"I look to a thousand years before,
when sages were in high position,
and none compare with Zhōu Gōng.
His Way was one,
the institutions were greatly complete,
and rulers after had something to follow.
I look to a thousand years after,
and none compare with Zhòngní,
whose Way was one,
but whose writings and teachings were luminous,
so that later scholars
had a standard for adjudication.
After a thousand years,
of those who explained the deeds of Zhōu Gōng,
I have not been able to meet them.
After a thousand years,
of those who continued the legacy of Xuānní,
I have not been able to yield to them."
The Master said:
"Cháng, perhaps, practices 'sitting in oblivion?'
In stillness, without confirming principle, he is sufficient for use;
in thought, sometimes subtle."
Lǐ Jìng asked about the Way of the sage.
The Master said:
"There is no path to it,
yet one does not arrive there."
A disciple said:
"Zhēng has arrived."
Someone said:
"Not yet."
The disciples were confused.
The Master said:
"Zhēng has left here,
but not reached there."
Someone asked about 'that.'
The Master said:
"'That'
is only one side of the Way. Must there be arrival?"
Dǒng Cháng was delighted to hear this, but the disciples did not understand.
Dǒng Cháng said:
"The Master's Way
comes with things,
and goes with things.
In coming, it has no origin;
in going, it looks nowhere."
Xuē Shōu said:
"How great is the Master's Way!
It is but one."
The Master said to Chéng Yuán:
"How do you compare with Dǒng Cháng?"
Chéng Yuán said:
"I dare not stand equal to Cháng.
Cháng manifests the Dao and virtue;
I only fix my will on benevolence and righteousness."
The Master said:
"That is indeed so for Cháng,
but as for your benevolence and righteousness,
they are not so constant.
As to 'that,' have you reached it?"
The Master said:
"Dǒng Cháng sometimes has deliberation,
while the rest harbor thoughts in movement and stillness."
The Master said:
"How filial is Xuē Shōu!
His conduct leaves no shame in life or death."
On days when the Master held mourning rites,
he did not smile the entire day."
Someone asked about Wáng Yǐn.
The Master said:
"He is a quick-witted man.
His capacity is bright,
his talent abundant,
and his learning ample."
Someone asked about his Way.
The Master said:
"His writings are many, but in institutions he is superficial;
his Way is not worthy of praise."
The Master said that Chén Shòu aspired to the records of history,
and, depending on great principle, expunged heresies.
He said that Fàn Níng aspired to the Chūnqiū,
and, attesting to the classics, questioned the multitude of traditions.
The Master said:
"If Chén Shòu was not renowned in history,
it was the fault of Qiān and Gù.
If Fàn Níng was not altogether admirable in the Chūnqiū,
it was the fault of Xīn and Xiàng."
Péi Xī said:
"What do you mean?"
The Master said:
"The failings of history
began from Qiān and Gù,
the records became verbose but the intent was scarce.
The loss in the Chūnqiū
began from Xīn and Xiàng,
who discarded the classic and relied on the traditions."
The Master said:
"After the rise of the Nine Schools, the Dao of the Yì became obscure;
after the three commentaries were written, the Chūnqiū was fragmented."
Jiǎ Qióng said:
"What do you mean?"
The Master said:
"Black and white confuse each other—
can subtlety be avoided?
Right and wrong entangle—
can fragmentation be avoided?"
"So the schools of Qí, Hán, Máo, and Zhèng—
they are the end of the Shī;
Great Dài and Small Dài—
they are the decline of the Lǐ.
The Shū is fragmented into ancient and modern texts,
the Shī lost in Qí and Lǔ.
Do you understand?"
Jiǎ Qióng said:
"Then should there be no schools or traditions?"
The Master said:
If the divine is enlightened,
it depends on the person.
If it is not the right person,
the Way will not proceed in vain.
Certainly, transmission is necessary,
and again it cannot be discarded.
The Master said to Shū Tián:
“Will you not compose the ‘Continued Book of Poetry’?”
Then, seeing the changes across seven generations,
he remained ultimately discontented.
The Master said:
“The ‘Continued Book of Poetry’ can be chanted,
can be conveyed,
can cleanse,
can be dwelt on in solitude;
when going out, it brings brotherliness,
when entering, it brings filial piety;
thus one often sees the conditions of order and disorder.”
Wén Zhōngzǐ said:
“My teacher
expressed himself fully in words, that is all.”
Someone asked about Yáng Xióng and Zhāng Héng.
The Master said:
“The remarkable men of antiquity,
their thoughts were laborious,
their words difficult.”
He asked:
“How was their Way?”
The Master said:
“In tranquility.”
The Master said:
“To err without adornment,
to violate without contention,
to have merit without boasting—
what a gentlemanly person!”
The Master said:
“I have yet to see one who rejoices at slander
and fears when praised.”
The Master said:
“In wealth, observe what one shares;
in poverty, observe what one takes;
in success, observe what one delights in;
in distress, observe what one does;
this suffices.”
Someone asked about Wèi Xiàowén.
The Master said:
“He could join in the transformation.”
The Lady of Tóngchuān was fond of medicines,
so the Master began composing formulas.
The Prefect of Ruìchéng esteemed yin and yang,
so the Master began writing on calendars.
Moreover, he said:
“I fear the reader may waste days.”
The Master regarded Xuē Zhīrén as good at dealing with the common world,
and married him to a daughter of Ruìchéng.
The Master said:
“To face inner difficulties and yet straighten one’s will—
this the Prefect of Tóngzhōu possessed.”
The Master said:
“As to the world,
I do not depart from it,
nor do I approach it;
I only follow the Way.”
Fáng Xuánlíng asked about the Way of serving one’s lord.
The Master said:
“Be without selfishness.”
He asked about the Way of employing others.
He said:
“Be without partiality.”
He asked:
“May I ask about the Way of transforming people?”
The Master said:
“Rectify one’s mind.”
He asked about ritual and music.
The Master said:
“When the kingly Way flourishes, then ritual and music rise with it;
this is not something within your reach.”
Someone asked about Yáng Sù.
The Master said:
“He creates fortune, wields authority, eats delicacies—
I know nothing else.”
Fáng Xuánlíng asked about the governance of prefectures and counties.
The Master said:
“The feudal states of the Zhōu dynasty lasted more than eight hundred years;
the Huáng Hàn’s fragmented reign endured over four hundred years;
since Wèi and Jìn,
disasters come too fast,
I do not know how they function.”
Yáng Sù sent someone to say to the Master:
“Why not accept office?”
The Master said:
“South of Shūshǔ,
at the bend of the Fēn River,
is my ancestor’s humble cottage,
which shields me from wind and rain;
there are fields enough to prepare gruel,
to play the qín and write books,
to discuss the Way and encourage righteousness—all for my own joy.
May you, my lord, regulate your conduct to unite the realm.
When times are peaceful and the years abundant,
the official system grants many rewards,
but I do not wish to serve.”
The Master said:
“Those who governed in antiquity
put virtue first and punishment second,
therefore their people were delighted and forgiving;
those who govern today
rely on punishment and neglect virtue,
so their people are resentful and deceitful.”
The Master said:
“In antiquity, those who took office provided for the people;
today, those who take office provide for themselves.”
The Master said:
“How grievous was the tyranny of Qí Wénxuān!”
Yáo Yì said:
“What does it mean to accomplish the end?”
The Master said:
“There was one, Yáng Zūnyàn,
who truly held the mandate of the state.
He regarded the people as if they were wounded;
how could he not be accomplished?”
Dòu Wēi was fond of discussing ritual.
The Master said:
“Was Wēi truly worthy?
I dare not say so.”
An Elder of Mount Běi said to Wén Zhōngzǐ:
“What does it mean for one who is restless
to have no urgency?”
The Master said:
“I dare not be urgent—
only lament that the times are idle.”
The Master said:
“I do not measure, do not hold fast;
do not persist, do not always succeed.”
Fáng Xuánlíng said:
“The Book says: Huò Guāng deposed and enthroned an emperor;
what does this mean?”
The Master said:
“Why only Huò Guāng?
In ancient times, great ministers,
when they deposed the dim and raised the wise,
thus brought peace to the world.”
The Master traveled to the islets of Héjiān.
An Elder from the River said:
“Why dwell here among these people?
Your heart seems intoxicated with the Six Classics,
your eyes seem to range across the four seas;
why dwell among these people?”
Wén Zhōngzǐ departed.
Xuē Shōu said:
“What sort of person is he?”
The Master said:
“A hermit.”
Shōu said:
“Why not follow him?”
The Master said:
“I have long not been able to keep pace with him.
Can a perfected one be followed?”
The Master said:
“No.”
The Master, by the river, said:
“Vast and flowing!
In former days I wished to stay here,
but could not attain it;
now I attain it, can I stay?”
The Master saw that officials and governors changed frequently,
and said:
“Yáo and Shùn took three years to review achievements;
Zhōngní accomplished results in three years.
Now they change in weeks or months—
I do not understand their Way.”
Xuē Shōu said:
"What do you think?"
The Master said:
"In the rise of the Three Dynasties,
each state and household had its own shèjì;
in the flourishing of the Two Hàn,
the regional governors had their own heirs.
It was not as urgent as that now.
To demand loyalty where there is no fixed lord,
to require transformation where there is no fixed populace—
even if one says he is able to accomplish it,
it will ultimately be without means."
Hè Ruòbì asked to shoot before the Master,
and upon shooting, he always hit the mark.
The Master said:
"How beautiful is skill in art!
In antiquity, the gentleman set his will upon the Way,
relied upon virtue,
depended upon humanity,
and only then could he freely roam in the arts."
Bì was displeased and withdrew.
The Master said to his disciples:
"Arrogant and obstinate:
such people will hardly escape trouble in today’s world."
The Master said of Xún Yuè:
"Historian, O Historian!" Of Lù Jī,
"Writer, O Writer!"
All their thoughts went beyond half-measures.
The Master said:
"The conduct of literary men can be observed:
Xiè Língyùn was a petty man!
His writings are proud;
a gentleman, by contrast, is careful.
Shěn Xiūwén was a petty man!
His writings are ornamental;
a gentleman, by contrast, is standard.
Bào Zhāo and Jiāng Yān
were the austere of old;
their writings are pressing and resentful.
Wú Jūn and Kǒng Guī
were the mad of old;
their writings are strange and angry.
Xiè Zhuāng and Wáng Róng
were the delicate of old;
their writings are fragmented.
Xú Líng and Yǔ Xìn
were the braggarts of old;
their writings are exaggerated.
Someone asked about the brothers of Xiào Chuò.
The Master said:
"Base men. Their writings are licentious."
Someone asked about the brothers of Xiāngdōng Wáng.
The Master said: "They are greedy men.
Their writings are overgrown."
Xiè Tiǎo,
a shallow man.
His writings are agile.
Jiāng Zǒng,
a devious man.
His writings are empty.
All these are not beneficial men of old."
The Master said:
"Yán Yánzhī, Wáng Jiǎn, and Rèn Fǎng
had the mind of a gentleman.
Their writings are restrained and measured."
The Grand Secretary summoned the Master for office.
The Master sent Yáo Yì to decline on his behalf.
He said:
"If I absolutely cannot avoid it,
assign me to Shǔ."
Someone said:
"That is remote."
The Master said:
"If I can spend my life wandering with Yán and Yáng,
why be concerned about remoteness?"
The Master said:
"I dislike the smooth-tongued;
must I then prefer the dull?
The dull do not act recklessly.
I dislike the bold;
must I then prefer the stingy?
The stingy do not scatter recklessly."
The Master said:
"How accomplished is Shān Tāo!
He approves much and criticizes little.
Someone asked:
'Is Wáng Róng wise?'
The Master said:
'If Róng is wise,
then none under heaven would not be wise.'"
The Master said:
"Chén Sī Wáng can be called one who understands principle;
he yielded the world,
but men of his time did not recognize him."
The Master said:
"A gentleman, indeed, was Sī Wáng!
His writings are deep and standard."
Fáng Xuánlíng asked about history.
The Master said:
"The historians of old discerned the Way;
historians now display their eloquence."
He asked about writing.
The Master said:
"The writings of old were restrained and expressive;
the writings of today are overwrought and stifling."
Xuē Shōu asked about the 'Continued Shī'.
The Master said:
"There are four names,
and there are five aims."
"What are the four names?"
"The first is 'transformation':
this is how the Son of Heaven exhorts all under heaven.
The second is 'government':
this is how vassal lords alter their customs.
The third is 'hymn':
to proclaim accomplishment to the spirits.
The fourth is 'lament':
to state admonition and establish warnings within the household."
"Of these four,
some are to praise,
some to exhort,
some to grieve,
some to criticize,
some to warn—
these are called the five aims."
The Master said to Shū Tián:
"Do you compose the Chūnqiū or Yuánjīng?
The Chūnqiū and Yuánjīng, in terms of the kings’ Way,
are the scales of lightness and heaviness,
the plumb line of right and wrong.
If they are lost, there is nothing by which to seek balance."
The Master said:
"The 'transformation' in the 'Continued Shī'
is perhaps like the 'elegant airs' in the kings’ poetry.
The 'government' in the 'Continued Shī'
is perhaps like the 'airs of the states' among the feudal lords."
The Master said:
"The governance of commanderies and counties—
how does it differ from the 'airs of the states'?
The 'airs of the states' are deep and firm;
the people are sincere.
They say:
'My lord does not urge me unduly;
thus there is harmony up and down.'
But when change comes,
there is toil and dispersal;
these people grieve at the thinness of the ruler's kindness,
yet do not dare to resent."
"The governance of commanderies and counties is pleasing, as by fortune;
the people long for it.
They say:
'My lord does not often comfort me;
so ministers and rulers are often replaced.'
But when change comes,
there is harshness and oppression;
these people resent the cruelty in the officials' hearts,
but there is nothing to grieve.
Even if there is good government,
it cannot be carried out."
Wèi Zhēng said:
"May I ask: when the 'airs of the states' change,
the people grieve but do not resent;
when the governance of commanderies and counties changes,
the people resent but do not grieve;
what does this mean?"
The Master said:
To be hurt without resentment,
one would not say, “He is still my ruler.”
If I could escape,
how could I dare to resent?
To resent without being hurt,
one would not say, “He is beneath me.”
If I intend to wrong him,
what harm is there?
Thus it is said: At the end of the Three Dynasties,
there was still humanity and righteousness preserved;
at the close of the Six Dynasties,
all humanity and righteousness were lost.
Why is this?
Those who led the people did not take the right path.
The Master said:
When the Airs and Odes change, the royal favor is exhausted;
when transformations and reforms arise, the imperial system declines.
The Master said:
If one’s words are fair but actions are contrary,
Wēn Yàn-Bó detested such;
If one praises face-to-face but slanders behind the back,
Wèi Zhēng detested such.
The Master said:
To cherish life and thereby destroy humanity—
is this not the conduct of those beneath the foolish?
To sacrifice oneself and thus fulfill humanity—
is this not the conduct of those among the worthy?
Among those who followed the gate of Zhōng Ní,
there was none who did not cultivate what is central.
Chén Shū-Dá was administrator of Jiàng Commandery;
he issued an order to arrest bandits, saying:
“Do not be hasty;
those who sincerely reform themselves shall be pardoned,
and we shall observe what comes after.”
On hearing this, the Master said:
“Governor Chén can be spoken to about government.”
When those above lose the Way,
the people disperse and it has been long so.
Were he not a gentleman,
how could he persist in adversity?
To guide with virtue,
to bind by trust,
and to observe what comes after—
is not this good?
Xuē Shōu asked:
“Bestowing kindness without harming righteousness,
practicing frugality without violating propriety—
how is this?”
The Master said:
“Even Wén and Jǐng were troubled by the difficulty of its practice.
To abolish corporal punishment harms righteousness;
to curtail it is permissible.
To wear unseasonal silks damages propriety;
to strike the mean is suitable.
Even so,
with the intent of Wén and Jǐng to carry it out, it is permissible;
but it cannot be the rule for later generations.”
The Master said:
“In ancient times one served the ruler by the Way,
if it was impossible, one would cease.
Today, those who serve the ruler do so by flattery,
there are no limits to what they will do.”
The Master said:
“As to my work on the ‘Notes to the Yì’,
I recounted but dared not criticize;
in ‘Rites’ and ‘Music’,
I discussed but dared not dispute;
in ‘Poetry’ and ‘Documents’,
I disputed but dared not question.”
Someone asked the reason.
The Master said:
“Some things are possible, some are not.”
He asked: “Does the Master himself have things possible and impossible?”
The Master said:
“Possible and impossible—
these are what are held by the world.
I am one who preserves what ought to be preserved.”
In leisure, the Master was reverent in appearance.
His movements were unhurried,
as though with something on his mind;
his bearing was upright,
as though he had something to fear.
His interactions with elders
were very respectful, as though never sufficient;
with the young,
he was gentle, as though nurturing.
The Master’s clothing was frugal and clean,
nothing superfluous;
brocade and embroidered silks
never entered his chamber.
He said:
“A gentleman does not wear yellow or white,
for women, green and blue are permitted.”
When the Master feasted with guests, there was never a second course;
in food, he always avoided the raw,
and flavors had to be appropriate.
He did not eat fruits or vegetables out of season,
saying:
“This is not in accord with Heaven’s order.”
If not from the local soil, he did not eat it,
saying:
“This is not in accord with earth’s order.”
In the village, if there was someone poor and in need,
he would say:
“If you take from me,
do not trouble your neighbors or the community,
I do not object.”
Whenever there was mourning in the village,
the Master would always go first,
and depart last.
In conversation, the Master responded but did not initiate;
when he initiated, it was on great matters.
There was no strife in the Master’s township.
When asked about someone’s goodness,
if the Master knew it to be good, he praised it;
if not,
he would say: “I have never been long acquainted with him.”
The Master, when crossing a great river,
would stop if there was wind;
he did not ascend heights,
he did not tread in danger,
he did not take ferocious mounts,
he did not drive with haste.
When there was community work involving water or earth,
he would take up his spade and go.
He said:
“I am not accompanying a great officer.”
At the mourning for the Lord of Tóngchuān Prefecture,
he did not take even a ladle of drink for three days.
Arranging the funeral,
he said:
“Be frugal,
for my family has its regulation.”
The coffin bore no adornment,
the body was wrapped in clothing and set forth,
a plain carriage was used,
a straw effigy on a simple cart,
thus no longer followed the custom of five generations past.
Once the burial was complete,
he said:
“From the time of Zhōng Ní,
there has never been a lack of intention.”
He then erected a mound,
four feet high,
without planting trees upon it.
When in another village,
at the home of the servant,
he would always inform them when going out or coming in.
Afterwards, he said:
“How can one go somewhere without notifying?”
At the village temple of Wànchūn,
the Master would always serve with care and diligence.
When the Lord of Ruìchéng Prefecture was first appointed as Surveillance Commissioner,
before his departure,
he said to Master Wén-Zhōng:
“What can you give me as a parting word?”
The Master said:
“Be pure, yet without aloofness;
upright, yet without obstinacy.”
He asked:
“What more?”
The Master said:
“Let utmost harmony be your outward standard;
sincerity your inner core.
Act with reverence,
hold fast to the Way.”
When he withdrew, he said to Dǒng Cháng:
“When a great hall is about to collapse,
it cannot be supported by a single pillar alone.”
Zǐ said:
To discuss wealth when arranging marriage,
this is the way of the yí and lǔ barbarians;
the jūnzǐ does not enter their villages.
In ancient times, the clans of men and women
each chose according to virtue,
not taking wealth as the standard of propriety.
Among the clans of Zǐ,
marriages unfailingly included the six rites.
He said:
This way,
now, is lost.
The foremost of the three bonds must not be discarded;
I follow the ancients.
Zǐ said:
To wear poor clothing and eat plain food,
to think little and desire little—
people today take this as deceit,
but I delight in such “deceit.”
Not showing off or boasting,
seeming dull or rustic—
people today see this as shameful,
but I do not feel shame in it.
Zǐ said:
In antiquity, to become an official
was to put into practice the Way;
but today, to become an official
is to indulge one’s desires.
How difficult it is!
Zǐ said:
For clerks to rise to office,
for the hardworking to be promoted,
this is not the way of the ancients;
is it not a cruel legacy of Qín?
In ancient times, the shì rose to office,
clerks handled labor,
salaries were to reward effort,
ranks were given for virtue.
Zǐ said:
How beautiful was Gōng Dàn in serving Zhōu!
Outwardly, he did not mind the world’s slander but guarded his conduct in private.
He said:
I must ensure that my descendants succeed one another,
such that the ancestral sacrifices do not end.
Inwardly, he comprehended the Way of the world and made his mind public.
He said:
I must ensure that my lord and ministers are at peace with each other,
such that disaster and chaos do not arise.
Profound, how profound!
Settling the family is what brings peace to the world.
Preserving myself is what fosters the people.
Therefore, the principle of moving the capital was thus:
The land of Luòyì,
is accessible in all directions and level,
making it easy for the virtuous to rise,
and easy for the unvirtuous to fall.
Wú Gōng wrote the "Account of Master Wǔdǒu."
Zǐ said:
Have you forgotten the world?
To indulge one’s emotions and break laws—
I cannot abide it.
Central Discourses, scroll three
Zǐ spoke of the Way of Zhōu Gōng:
Bent yet appropriate,
private yet compassionate.
In his fathoming of principle and full realization of nature, he arrived at destiny!
Zǐ said:
The Way of the sage:
its flourishing is hidden,
its decline is gradual,
proceeding quietly like the coming and going of cold and heat;
all things follow it,
yet know not whence it arises.
Wēn Yànbó asked:
Who were Jī Kāng and Ruǎn Jí?
Zǐ said:
They were renowned reasoners of old,
but could not reach the utmost.
He asked:
What do you mean?
Zǐ said:
Their Way was insufficient, but skill in artifice abounded.
He replied:
Dare I ask what is meant by Way and instrument?
Zǐ said:
To master transformation is called Way;
to hold to the fixed is called instrument.
He asked:
Who was Liú Líng?
Zǐ said:
He was a reclusive man of old.
He said:
Is this acceptable?
He replied:
To forget the world altogether—
is this not also acceptable?
He asked:
Is the Way sufficient?
He replied: If so, I do not know it.
Chén Shǒu said to Xuē Shēng:
I issue orders in commanderies and counties and banditry does not cease,
but when you, Master, dwell in the village, contention quiets—
why is this?
Xuē Shēng said:
It is transformation by words in this case,
but by heart in that.
Chén Shǒu said:
I have erred.
He retired to stillness,
and after three months, the bandits left the region.
When Zǐ heard of this, he said:
Cherish worthy words;
Shū Dá is truly of excellent virtue.
Fáng Xuánlíng asked:
Tián Chóu—who was he?
Zǐ said:
A man of righteousness in antiquity.
Zǐ spoke of
the Wǔdé dance as diligent and decisive.
Its plans and deliberations:
did they pass through the Son of Heaven!
And of
the Zhāodé dance, as composed and at ease.
Its harmonious spirit and regulated energy:
did they pacify the world?
The governor of Tàiyuán said:
What do you think?
Zǐ said:
Some achieve by decisive action,
others keep by tranquil maintenance.
I do not know their transformation.
Alas!
Wǔdé:
its merits remain,
but it is not as good as the excellence of Zhāodé.
Moreover, the imperfection of Wǔdé has long persisted.
Is it not time!
Is it not time!
Zǐ spoke of
Shǐ Tán skillfully recounting the nine schools;
he knew they could not be discarded,
yet knew each had its faults.
Where can one find a sage’s advice?
Zǐ said:
By understanding transformations,
no law in the world is flawed;
by clinging to the fixed,
no teaching in the world is good.
Therefore it is said:
It depends on the person.
Zǐ said:
Where can I find a man of flexible understanding
to discuss the nine schools together?
Where can I find a sovereign of imperial balance
to describe the nine principles with him together?
Dù Yán asked:
Who was Cuī Hào?
Zǐ said:
He overpowered others.
He clung to minor paths
and disrupted the great order.
Chéng Yuán said:
Dare I ask, what is the “Bīn Fēng”?
Zǐ said:
It is a transformed air.
Yuán said:
At the time of Zhōu Gōng,
was there also a transformed air?
Zǐ said:
When lord and minister rebuke one another,
how can things be set aright?
As King Chéng ended with doubt,
the air thus transformed.
If it were not for Zhōu Gōng’s utmost sincerity,
who could have completed it to the end?
Yuán said:
“‘Bīn’ is placed at the end of the ‘Transforming Airs’;
why is this so?”
The Master said:
From King Yí and below,
the ‘Transforming Airs’ could no longer be rectified.
The Master lamented this,
and therefore concluded with the “Airs of Bīn.”
This speaks to the possibility of rectifying change,
which only Zhōu Gōng could achieve.
Thus, he connected it with correctness;
the singing of Bīn proclaims: this is the root of Zhōu.
Alas,
if not for Zhōu Gōng, who would know its hardship?
To transform and yet manage to rectify,
to be in peril and yet able to support,
from beginning to end not losing the root—
is this not Zhōu Gōng alone?
How far-reaching is the connection with Bīn!
The Master said:
When Qí Huán honored the royal house,
feudal lords submitted;
only Guǎn Zhòng understood this.
When Fú Qín declared the great title,
and the Central Plain became tranquil,
only Wáng Měng understood this.
Someone said
Fú Qín was rebellious.
The Master said:
This was the crime of the Jìn system of appointment,
how was Fú Qín rebellious?
In former times, the Zhōu system conferred powers equitably in the name of the public,
so Qí Huán and Guǎn Zhòng could not defy it.
The Jìn system made appointments according to private favor,
so Fú Qín and Wáng Měng could not serve it.
Thus they responded to Heaven, followed fate, secured the state, and relieved the people!
Therefore King Wǔ did not dare defy Heaven’s mandate nor abandon the people to serve Zhòu,
Qí Huán did not dare defy Heaven’s mandate nor abandon the people to depose Zhōu.
Thus it is said:
it was the crime of Jìn;
how was Fú Qín rebellious?
For more than thirty years,
the scholars and commoners of China,
east, west, south, and north,
came from afar,
this was due to Měng’s ability.
The Master said:
As for Fú Qín having a minister,
was it not by the deeds of Wáng Měng?
For Yuán Wèi having a ruler,
was it not by the deeds of Xiào Wén?
The Way of China was not lost,
this was by the effort of Xiào Wén.
Tàiyuán Prefect said:
What kind of person was Wēn Zǐshēng?
The Master said:
A dangerous man.
His wisdom was too small for his grand schemes.
Regarding the matter of Yǒng’ān,
the Lord of Tóngzhōu often gnashed his teeth over it,
so there must have been reason.
The Master read about the deeds of the Three Founders.
He said:
How diligent they were,
but to no avail!
Do not say that Wèi and Zhōu had no worthy men,
only my house did not employ them.
In the Master’s ancestral temple,
the seat always faces to the southeast,
this started with Duke Mù.
He said:
He had not yet recorded his ancestor’s domain.
The campaign in Liáodōng—
the Master heard of it and said:
Disaster began from this point.
The Son of Heaven did not heed Bó Yì’s praise of Yǔ’s words,
the high ministers did not employ the case of Wèi Xiàng’s admonition of Emperor Xuān.
Wáng Xiàoyì said to the Master:
All under Heaven contend for profit and abandon righteousness,
what can I alone do?
The Master said:
To set aside what they contend for,
and choose what they cast away,
is this not the mark of a gentleman?
The Master said to Jiǎ Qióng, Wáng Xiàoyì, and Líng Jìng:
What delights do you all have?
Jiǎ Qióng said:
The delight of dwelling in leisure.
The Master said:
To be tranquil and reflect upon the Way, this is fitting.
Wáng Xiàoyì said:
The delight of hearing one’s faults.
The Master said:
When faults are often heard,
it is beneficial.
Líng Jìng said:
The delight of meeting good people.
The Master said:
Is it not a joy to have many worthy men?
Xuē Shōu traveled in Guǎntáo,
and happened to return with Wèi Zhēng.
He informed the Master:
Zhēng is a vessel fit for Yán and Rǎn.
Zhēng lodged at the Master’s residence,
expounded the ‘Six Classics,’
and did not go out for over a month.
When he left,
he said to Xuē Shōu:
Though a luminous ruler did not appear, yet the Master lived—
thus the Three Powers and Nine Categories belonged to the men of plain attire.
Liú Xuàn met the Master
and discussed the ‘Six Classics.’
Raising a single topic,
the whole day could not exhaust it.
The Master said:
How much he has.
Xuàn said:
The differences and agreements among former scholars
cannot but be recounted.
The Master said:
It is enough to connect all with one thread.
Do you believe Confucius was one who recognized all through wide learning?
When Xuàn withdrew,
the Master said to his disciples:
His words are splendid,
his Way attains but little—
how hard it is!
Líng Jìng asked about the root of rites and music.
The Master said:
Without deceit.
When Líng Jìng withdrew,
the Master said:
Worthy indeed, this scholar!
To ask about rites and music as the foundation.
The Master said:
The “Great Wind” did not forget danger in peace—
is that not the resolve of a hegemon?
“Autumn Wind”—in utmost joy comes sorrow—
is that not the first stirring of regret?
The Master said:
When ‘The Odes’ and ‘The Documents’ flourished but perished in Qín times,
this was not the fault of Zhòngní;
when empty abstraction flourished and the Jìn house fell into disorder,
this was not the fault of Lǎo and Zhuāng;
when purification and abstinence held sway yet Liáng perished,
this was not the fault of Shìjiā.
Does not the ‘Yì’ say:
If it is not the right person,
the Way will not move forward in vain.
Someone asked about Buddha.
The Master said:
A sage.
He asked:
What is his teaching like?
He said:
It is the teaching of the West.
In China, it is already stuck in the mud.
Chariots and carriages cannot reach Yuè lands,
ceremonial caps cannot be worn among the Hú—
such was the Way of antiquity.
Someone asked about Yǔwén Jiǎn.
The Master said:
A gentleman scholar.
Broad and clear, far-reaching in understanding—
is this not the depth of his work in ‘The Documents’?
Prefect of Tóngchuān esteemed him,
how could this be without reason?
The Master went to the Grand Music,
and heard the tune of “Dragon Boat at Dawn,”
whereupon he looked startled and left.
He said:
This is dissipated music.
If played in states and regions,
it will not do for public gatherings.
The Master spoke to Yáo Yì:
“Why not take office?”
Yì said:
“To abandon the Way for the pursuit of rank,
Yì has not had the leisure.”
The Master said:
“How true!”
Someone asked about Xún Yù and Xún Yōu.
The Master said:
“Both are worthy men.”
He asked:
“How were their lives and deaths?”
The Master said:
“They lived to save their age,
and died to manifest the Way;
the Xún lineage has two men of benevolence.”
The Master said:
“To speak and be trusted
is not as good as to be trusted without speaking;
to act with caution
is not as good as to be cautious without acting.”
Jiǎ Qióng said:
“How is this so?”
The Master said:
“Promote sincerity,
then trust is without need of words;
pacify with calmness,
then caution is had without action.
Only one who possesses the Way can do this.”
Yáng Sù said to the Master:
“How excessive it was,
the ancient custom of hats, robes, garments, and shoes:
how simple yet impractical.”
The Master said:
“The ceremonial dress of the former kings—
was it not profound?
Hats were to dignify the head,
shoes to honor the feet.
The garments were loose,
the sword and ornaments resonated,
all to prevent recklessness.
Thus it is said they were solemn,
and men looked on them with awe.
Using this to restrain the people,
still some would dash wildly on the road.
Now abandoning it as inconvenient,
is like casting fish into the abyss,
or putting apes among trees.
How can the world not indulge in reckless abandon?
Those who lead them are not following the Way.”
Dǒng Cháng sang “Bǎi Zhōu” from the Book of Songs.
The Master heard it and said:
“Heaven indeed brings it about,
what can one say of it?”
Pī Gōng delighted in ancient objects,
collecting bells, tripods, jade tablets, imperial seals, and coins, none were lacking.
The Master heard and said:
“The ancients who loved antiquity gathered the Way;
those now who love antiquity gather wealth.”
The Master said to Zhòngcháng Zǐguāng:
“Is it possible to live in the mountains and forests?”
He replied:
“When occasion meets what is fitting,
who can know if it is possible?”
The Master said:
“You are a man of understanding—
to live in seclusion and speak without restraint!”
When Zǐguāng withdrew, he said to Dǒng and Xuē:
“Is not your teacher
a perfected man?
To him, life and death are one,
one cannot alter his mind.”
Xuē Shōu asked about withdrawal.
The Master said:
“The perfected man hides in Heaven,
next is to hide in earth,
next to hide in fame.”
The Master said that Yáo Yì was skilled in friendship.
Someone said
he was reserved.
The Master said:
“That is what makes him skilled.”
Someone said
he was expansive.
The Master said:
“Expansive yet not indiscriminate—
that too makes him skilled.”
The Master said:
“Cháo Cuò set the order of the well-field system,
truly intent on restoring antiquity.”
Jiǎ Qióng asked about the meaning of the ‘Continued Documents.’
The Master said:
“There are four categories of Imperial Orders as set forth:
edict,
decree,
record,
and admonition.
There are seven categories of orders issued by great ministers in their activities:
appointment,
instruction,
reply,
commendation,
deliberation,
warning,
and remonstrance.”
Wén Zhōngzǐ said:
“The system of the Emperor
is vast and all-encompassing.
If he has great systems,
can he order all under Heaven without partition?
Above, he is serene;
below, he is calm.
The perils of the world,
he shares in securing it;
the losses of the world,
he helps rectify them.
Amidst myriad changes,
I always keep to the mean.
Can it be exalted and immovable?
Can it be responsive and universally connected? This is called the Emperor’s system.”
Wén Zhōngzǐ said:
“The concerns and anxieties of the Book of Changes
are cautious,
and diligent.
Its fear of Heaven and pity for the people,
its thinking and acting in accord with the times.
Fán Shīxuán said:
‘How distant,
when I look at the Way of the Changes,
how difficult it is!’
The Master laughed and said:
‘Is it really so?
To be diligent all day is possible.
If I see something unworthy,
my thoughts do not stray far.’
Yuè Gōng summoned the Master.
The Master said to his envoy:
‘To maintain and put into practice is enough.’
He sang “Gàn Máo” to send him off.
Afterwards he said:
‘Is this about jade and silk?’
The Master said to Fáng Xuánlíng:
“Fondness for completion
is the root of failure;
longing for what is broad
leads to narrowness.”
Xuánlíng asked:
“How is it to establish merit and establish words?”
The Master said:
“One must surely measure one’s strength!”
The Master said:
“Yáo Yì may be befriended—
long bonds not forgotten;
Jiǎ Qióng may be employed in action—
unshaken in difficulty;
Xuē Shōu may serve his lord—
benevolent and not glib;
Dǒng Cháng may handle both advancement and retirement—
steadfast as he is.”
The Master said:
“To despise things and value oneself—
a gentleman does not do so.
To crave novelty and prize the strange,
letting oneself go without end,
must certainly be in answer to an ignoble mind.”
Xuē Hóng requested to view the Six Classics,
but the Master did not bring them out.
The students were perplexed.
The Master laughed and said:
“For a gentleman who loves antiquity and is widely learned,
there is nothing I would conceal.”
The Master’s wife’s younger brother died;
he did not drink wine or eat meat.
The people of the commandery criticized this.
The Master said:
“I cannot bear otherwise.”
He recited the last stanza of ‘Zài Chí’ and departed.
Zhèng Hé slandered Zǐ before Yuè Gōng, saying:
“He is truly disrespectful to your lordship,
why do you value him so highly?”
Yuè Gōng sent someone to question Zǐ.
Zǐ said:
“If your lordship may be slighted,
then I stand to gain;
if your lordship may not be slighted,
then I lose.
Gaining or losing pertains to me—
what does it concern your lordship?”
Thereafter, Yuè Gōng treated him as before.
Zǐ said:
“I have not yet seen a courageous person.”
Someone said,
“Hè Ruòbì.”
Zǐ said:
“Bì is wayward;
how can he be called courageous?”
Lǐ Mì asked about heroes.
Zǐ said:
“He who knows himself is a hero,
he who overcomes himself is mighty.”
He asked about courage.
Zǐ said:
“Surely, it must be a matter of righteousness?”
Jiǎ Qióng said:
“Truly, few in the world understand you, sir.”
Zǐ said:
“Do you really wish them to understand?
For now, cultivate yourself,
and Heaven will make it known—
how much more will men?”
Jiǎ Qióng asked for the original of the Six Classics,
saying:
“I fear your Way, Master, may perish.”
Zǐ said:
“Are you seeking fame?
If one has beautiful jade, let him wait for the right price.”
Yáng Xuángǎn asked about filial piety.
Zǐ said:
“It begins with service to one's parents,
and ends with the establishment of one's own character.”
He asked about loyalty.
Zǐ said:
“When filial piety is established, then loyalty will follow.”
Liú Xuàn asked about the Yì.
Zǐ said:
“The sage with respect to the Yì—
only when life ends is it complete,
how much more it must be so for us.”
Xuàn said:
“When discussing it at court,
there is no one who matches me.”
Zǐ did not answer.
Upon withdrawing, he said to his disciples:
“Complete it in silence,
be trustworthy without speaking,
hold firm to virtue and conduct.”
Wèi Zhēng said:
“Do sages experience anxiety?”
Zǐ said:
“If all under Heaven are anxious,
can I alone be without anxiety?”
He asked about doubt.
Zǐ said:
“If all under Heaven have doubts,
can I alone be without doubt?”
Zhēng withdrew.
Zǐ said to Dǒng Cháng:
“To delight in Heaven and know one’s destiny—
what cause have I to worry?
If one exhausts principle and fulfills one’s nature—
what cause have I to doubt?”
Cháng said:
“Did you not say so to Zhēng?
Do you, sir, speak with two voices?”
Zǐ said:
“Zhēng’s questions concern outward traces;
my words to you concern the heart.
The separation between heart and traces is long established;
can I alone speak with but one voice?”
Cháng said:
“Are heart and traces inherently different?”
Zǐ said:
“From your perspective, they are indeed different,
but those who reach attainment do not perceive their difference,
each merely says what is fitting.
So, the seeming duality does not violate unity.”
Lǐ Bō heard and sighed, saying:
“How great is unity!
All beneath Heaven return to it,
yet are unaware.”
Chéng Yuán asked Shū Tián:
“In the Xùshū, there are ‘zhì’ and ‘zhào’—
what do they mean?”
Shū Tián related this to Wén Zhōngzǐ.
Zǐ said:
“‘Zhì’ completes the Way;
words express one’s resolve.
An edict gives expression to the king’s intent!
Such solicitude for the people is extensive,
and he fully commits himself to their use.
With one word, all under Heaven respond;
with one order, none may alter it.
Unless one is vastly benevolent and wise,
so that Heaven’s mandate is clearly known,
who is able to edict the world?”
Shū Tián said:
“May I ask, what is a cè (policy paper)?”
Zǐ said:
“Its words are orthodox,
its reach is broad,
compassionate yet not self-serving,
laboring without weariness;
such indeed is the cè!”
Zǐ said:
“How profound are the commands in the Xùshū:
there are outlines for sovereigns and ministers,
suited to their times.
It contains both success and failure,
and all under Heaven are suspended by its guidance,
thus they cannot but comply.
In advancing and retreating, waxing and waning,
its crucial moment is never missed.
The Way is exceedingly great,
nothing is excluded,
it goes forth lofty and solitary,
yet fits the transformations most precisely—
truly a self-made mandate of Heaven!”
Wén Zhōngzǐ said:
“In affairs,
should one not take counsel of benevolence and righteousness and be prudent in design?
Even the Son of Heaven must have teachers;
yet is there truly always a fixed teacher?
Wherever the Way resides—
take the body of all under Heaven,
accept the instruction of all under Heaven,
attain the Way of all under Heaven,
accomplish the tasks of all under Heaven—
the people do not know how it is achieved;
such is the enlightened ruler!”
Wén Zhōngzǐ said:
“To broaden benevolence and increase wisdom,
nothing is better than questioning;
to apply matters and elaborate the Way,
nothing is better than response.
Who but an enlightened ruler can widely inquire?
Who but a capable minister can devote himself to responding?
To follow what is fitting and draw analogies,
there is nothing unexamined!
Expansive indeed—
are the answers of Cháo, Dǒng, and Gōngsūn!”
Wén Zhōngzǐ said:
“If beauty is not displayed,
how can the world behold it?
A worthy, towards the ruler,
praises his virtues and corrects his faults.
Thus, there is not even time enough to advance the good;
how could the world then be at unrest?”
Wén Zhōngzǐ said:
“Discussion—
does it not exhaust all minds under Heaven?
In ancient times, Huángdì had the Assembly Palace for counsel,
Yáo had the Crossroads Chamber for inquiry,
Shùn had the General Audience Chamber for consultation—
all denote discussion.
How great this is! To unite all strategies under Heaven,
to combine all the wisdom of the world,
and thus realize order.
For myself, what more need I do?
Only respectfully sit facing south as sovereign.”
The Master said:
The human heart is ever precarious,
the heart that follows Dào is ever subtle;
it is difficult to advance along the Way through words.
Therefore, the junzǐ reflects on mistakes and guards against them beforehand;
this is why there are admonitions.
Be earnest without pointing fingers,
diligent without complaint,
accommodating without flattery,
upright yet courteous—
is this not admonition indeed!
The Master said:
To correct one's faults without hesitation,
he who is free from blame is one who is good at making amends.
The enlightened kings of antiquity—
could they really be without fault?
They simply listened to remonstrance.
Therefore, when a loyal minister serves his lord,
he exhausts his loyalty to make amends for faults.
If the lord errs above,
the minister compensates from below;
if the minister remonstrates from below,
the lord complies from above.
This is why the royal Way does not collapse.
To find peace in adversity,
to exchange darkness for clarity—
who but the remonstrators can reach this!
Wénzhōngzǐ said:
Since the Jìn dynasty and after,
why have there been so many contending lords and disorder?
Looking on Huì and Huái, I grieve for them;
apart from the Three Kingdoms, where can one find steadfast will?
How those Three Kingdoms toiled anxiously, ever beset by worries!
Looking on Huán and Líng, I am pained for them;
apart from the Two Hàn, where can one find true governance?
The Master remarked that the administration of Tàihé was close to uprightness,
and once made clear that Zhōngguó had laws.
Alas,
it was not possible to follow the Way of Mù Gōng.
Chéng Yuán said:
What of the Three Teachings?
The Master said:
Long have politics been spoiled by many divisions.
He said:
What if they were abolished?
The Master said:
That is beyond your reach.
The deeds of Zhēn Jūn and Jiàn Dé
only serve to stir the waves higher,
to fan the flames of the winds.
The Master read the "Hong Fan Dang Yi".
He said:
Thus can the Three Teachings be united.
Chéng Yuán and Wèi Zhēng came forward and said:
Why is this so?
The Master said:
So that the people will not grow weary.
Jiǎ Qióng studied the Book of Documents,
and when he came to the story of Zhì Yùn,
he asked the Master, saying:
May I inquire about the difference between shì ("event"), mìng ("destiny"), zhì ("will"), and zhì ("regulation")?
The Master said:
Regarding regulation and destiny,
I set forth their principles;
regarding will and event, I set forth their standards.
Jiǎ Qióng conveyed this to Shū Tián.
Shū Tián said:
Has the Book of Documents omitted nothing?
The Book of Documents says:
"Be pure and unified,
truly grasp the Mean."
Is this not speaking of principle?
The Book of Songs says:
"Pick radish greens, pick cress,
do not degrade what is below."
Is this not speaking of standards?
When the Master heard this, he said:
His understanding of the Book of Documents is solid indeed.
The Master said:
The relation of "event" to "destiny"
is like that of "will" to "regulation".
If benevolence and righteousness do not arise from within,
success cannot be achieved.
The Master said:
He who comprehends the principles of regulation and destiny,
would he not understand the deeds of kings and lords?
Would he not gain insight into transformation?
He who understands the principles of will and event,
would he not know the difficulties between ruler and minister?
Would he not grasp the subtlety of benevolence and righteousness?
The Master said:
To dwell in poverty and lowliness without fear,
this makes one worthy of wealth and honor;
if servants speak of your kindness,
you are fit to govern;
if friends speak of your trustworthiness,
your achievements may be established.
The Master said:
To love fame and value profit—
what a petty man!
Never have I seen a man of benevolence who loved fame and profit.
Jiǎ Qióng asked about the Way of the junzǐ.
The Master said:
If you do not reflect and change,
let it end there.
When the Master saw one in mourning attire weeping without ceasing,
he went to offer condolences.
He asked about the period of mourning.
He replied:
It has been five years.
The Master, his eyes wet with tears, said:
The institutions of the former kings must not be transgressed.
Duke Chǔ asked about the way to use an army.
The Master said:
Act with benevolence and righteousness.
He asked:
How can victory be determined?
The Master said:
Nothing surpasses benevolence and righteousness.
Go beyond this,
and you invite defeat.
Whenever the Master saw farmers, he always comforted them in their toil;
when he met royal officials, he always bowed to them.
He never rode horseback in his native village;
when the rooster first crowed,
he washed, rinsed his mouth, and dressed in proper attire.
When the Lady of Tóngchuān was ill,
the Master did not lie down to sleep for three months.
Whenever someone came to inquire after her, in seeing them off and welcoming them,
he always wept and bowed.
The Master said:
Since the rise of histories and biographies, the Way of the Classics has been neglected;
since the rise of notes and commentaries, the discipline of the historians has been slandered.
Therefore, he despised such heterodox teachings.
Xuē Shōu said:
What is destiny?
The Master said:
Investigate it in Heaven,
harmonize it among people,
observe that what is fixed here echoes there.
Good and ill, twists and turns,
there is nowhere to escape!
Without being a junzǐ,
who can know and fear it?
Without being a sage,
who can attain it?
Xuē Shōu said: In antiquity, men composed "Yuánmìng"; could they have attained it? The Master said: They attained it.
Jiǎ Qióng said:
In the Book of Documents there is regulation but not destiny—
why is this?
The Master said:
Could there be ministers in the world without a sovereign?
He said:
But the Two Hàn have both regulation and will—
how is this?
The Master said:
Regulation—
was it not perfected by compassion for the people?
Will—
was it not humbled in virtue by provision of all things?
Xuē Shōu said:
Does imperial regulation depart from the royal Way?
The Master said:
It cannot depart.
The emperors of later times
were not the same as the emperors of the past.
They mingled the ways of a hundred kings,
yet took for themselves the name of Emperor.
Their hearts were upright,
but their actions were devious.
They inherited Qín's failures
and had no choice but to bear the name.
As for governance, if it is handled carelessly and simply,
how could it compare to the pure excellence of the three eras of Tāng, Yú, and the Three Dynasties?
Thus, it is acceptable for men of wealth,
but not for rituals and ceremony.
Xuē Shōu said,
“Has pure excellence then perished?”
The Master said,
“It is people who can broaden the Way;
how do you know that those who come after will not equal those of old?”
The Master said that Lǐ Jìng excelled in wisdom over benevolence,
while Chéng Yuán excelled in benevolence over wisdom.
The Master said that Dǒng Cháng was close to the Way,
and could effect change in principle.
Jiǎ Qióng asked,
“How may one cease slander?”
The Master said,
“By not arguing.”
Qióng said,
“How may one halt resentment?”
The Master said,
“By not contending.”
The Master said of Zhūgě and Wáng Měng,
“Their achievements are near, but their virtue is far off.”
When the Master was at Pú,
he heard of the defeat at Liáodōng.
He said to Xuē Shōu,
“The city has again returned to ruin.”
He recited the final stanza of ‘Tù Yuán’.
On his return, he admired the roots of the Six Classics,
and said,
“Let this await those who are able.”
The Master said,
“Those who are fond of action encounter many difficulties.
Failing in small forbearance
brings about great disaster.”
The Master said,
“The Yì Jīng—
the movement of the sage
is to apply it in keeping with the times.
Thus, the hexagrams
are the dwelling place of wisdom,
and the sequence of action.”
Xuē Shēng said,
“Can wisdom act alone?”
The Master said,
“It must be guarded with benevolence.
If one cannot be benevolent, wisdom ceases,
so how could it be put into use?”
The Master said,
“Central, prosperous, favorable, and upright.
Its unending operation
is the work of wisdom.”
The Master said,
“Flattery is used to serve superiors;
cruelty to control inferiors;
enticing them with righteousness will not move them.”
When Dǒng Cháng died,
the Master wept for him,
a whole day without ceasing.
His disciples asked,
“Why do you mourn so deeply?”
He said,
“I mourn that Heaven does not support the Way.
Now that this man has died,
I too shall soon depart.
Even if an enlightened king arises,
he cannot establish the rites and music.”
The Master praised the Yì Jīng,
and when he reached the ‘Sequence of the Hexagrams’,
he said,
“Great indeed
is the succession of the times!
Those who are insightful may engage with the subtle.”
When he reached the ‘Miscellaneous Hexagrams’,
he said,
“To travel to the side without being swept away—
those who stand firm may keep righteous purpose.”
The Master said,
“Name and reality give rise to each other,
benefit and use complete each other,
right and wrong clarify each other,
going and staying are at peace with each other.”
Jiǎ Qióng asked,
“Can great peace be attained?”
The Master said,
“The codes of the Five Constants,
proclamations of the Three Kings,
institutions of the Two Hàn,—
all clearly visible.”
Wénzhōngzǐ said,
“When royal favor is exhausted, the lords rely on righteousness;
when imperial authority declines, all under Heaven speak of profit.”
Wénzhōngzǐ said,
“Strong states contest by force;
hegemon states by wit;
kingly states by righteousness;
imperial states by virtue;
sovereign states by non-action.
If the Son of Heaven contests by force,
then the way of kingship and hegemony cannot stand,
so how could he bear the name of emperor?
Thus, when imperial power perishes, name and substance are scattered.”
The Master said,
“Much talk
is the thief of virtue;
much doing
makes an enemy of life.”
Xuē Fāngshì said,
“When meeting evil, denounce it;
when encountering depravity, correct it;
what of this?”
The Master said,
“Might this not bring about a wrongful death?
What is essential is that words have no fault,
and what is heard serves as a warning.”
Someone asked about Wéi Xiàokuān.
The Master said,
“Capable.”
(They) asked about Yáng Yīn.
The Master said,
“Supportive.”
Yǔwén Huàjí asked about the way of Heaven and the affairs of men.
The Master said,
“Accord with yīn and yáng, with humaneness and righteousness—
that is all.”
Jiǎ Qióng served as an official,
and attended on Chǔ Gōng in his duties.
When he was about to depart,
the Master saw him off.
Qióng said,
“May I hear the way of serving others?”
The Master said,
“Be distant without harboring enmity,
approach without flattery.
Speak generally of profit and offer remonstrance,
do not compete for quick success.”
Qióng said,
“I will recite this all my life.”
The Master said,
“It would be well to practice it all your life.”
The Master said,
“‘The Yuan Classic’ sets names right!
The emperors at the beginning drew on Heaven to impart it.
The rulers of Jìn and Sòng
were close to the true form,
and so did not forget Zhōngguó,
which was the aspiration of Mù Gōng.
The virtue of Qí, Liáng, and Chén
was pushed to the four barbarians,
thus revealing that Zhōngguó had changed dynasties,
by the power of Great Harmony.”
The Master said,
“Changing the reign-title and establishing a new name
is not of the ancients;
it surely arises in the hearts of those men themselves.”
Someone asked,
“If one’s purpose is cultivated,
one despises wealth and rank;
if one values the Way and righteousness,
one scorns kings and lords—
how is that?”
The Master said,
“Such a one has what he relies on to preserve himself.”
Xuē Shēng said:
“After the death of Shāng,
the imperial system was severed.
Why then did the Yuánjīng not arise?”
The Master said:
“As for the imperial system,
the gentleman waits with unified mind and single breath.
He listens intently,
and wipes his eyes to see clearly;
thus he grants it time in years and seasons.
At the juncture of Huán and Líng,
the imperial system perished.
At the juncture of Wén and Míng,
was not the Wèi system yet unformed?
At the beginning of Tài Kāng,
writing was unified,
and carriages shared the same tracks.
The gentleman said:
‘The imperial system could be established,
but it could not be revived.’
Thus after Yǒngxī,
the gentleman ceased to hope.”
He said:
“How should this be called?
Was it that the Yuánjīng arose out of necessity?”
Wénzhōngzǐ said:
“When the Chūnqiū was composed, the Diǎn and Gào ceased;
when the Yuánjīng flourished, the imperial system perished.”
Wénzhōngzǐ said:
“The feudal lords do not offer poems,
the Son of Heaven does not gather folksongs,
the music officials do not convey the refined airs,
the national historians do not clarify political change.
Alas!
Such has it been for long.
Can the Shī be left uncontinued?”
End of the scroll
