The Master said:
“As for rites and music,
I have only missed the correct path.
As for their composition,
I await a sage of great wisdom—
must they be honored and revered?”
Jiǎ Qióng and Xuē Shōu said:
“When the Way does not prevail,
what then?”
The Master said:
“Let parents be at ease,
brothers cherish one another,
friends be trustworthy.
If this is practiced in government,
the Way also prevails;
why say that it does not?”
The Master remarked:
“The ignobility of Rèn, Xuē, Wáng, Liú, Cuī, and Lú is not in accord with antiquity;
why look to genealogies?”
Wénzhōngzǐ said:
“It has long been that the Emperor is not truly Emperor.”
Wáng Xiàoyì said:
“May I ask, in the Yuánjīng, what is meant by ‘Emperor’?”
The Master said:
“Rectifying names and seeking for substance—
this cannot be discarded.
As for being Emperor,
the substance is lost but the name remains.”
Someone asked about Xiè Ān.
The Master said:
“He was simple.”
They asked about Wáng Dǎo.
The Master said:
“He was respectful.”
They asked about Wēn Jiǎo.
The Master said:
“He was a resolute man.”
They asked about Huán Wēn.
The Master said:
“His wisdom was near, his schemes were far;
few can match him.”
Jiǎ Qióng asked about the Way of living in groups.
The Master said:
“Harmony does not harm what is correct;
difference does not injure others.”
He asked:
“Can this be practiced for life?”
The Master said:
“Why could it not be?
Those who had the Way in antiquity
were true within,
yet outwardly differed not from custom.
Thus they were whole.”
Fán Shīxuán said:
“Dare I ask about the benefit of consulting antiquity?”
The Master said:
“Is it to uphold the ancient in order to resist the present?”
The Master said:
“By residing near, one understands the distant;
by living in the present, one knows the ancient—
this is none but through learning.”
The Master said:
“With respect, things obey;
with honesty, there is accomplishment;
with balance, things are transformed.”
The Master said:
“I have yet to see one who is truly balanced.”
Someone said:
“It is enough that the gentleman is benevolent;
what need of rites?”
The Master said:
“It cannot be done.”
Someone said:
“Were rites established for people like us?”
The Master did not answer,
but then said to Xuē Shōu:
“Such a man
walks sideways but does not drift;
how can he know the intent of teaching?
Yǒu Ruò said that the Way of the Former Kings
is excellent.”
Wénzhōngzǐ said:
“When the master of the seven systems holds sway,
the Way flourishes.”
Xuē Shōu said:
“Why is this so?”
The Master said:
“Alas!
Only an enlightened king can accept instruction.”
Shōu said:
“If there is instruction but no system,
what does this mean?”
The Master said:
“Is it that the system of the former Emperors has not yet perished?
Are the mandates of the great ministers still upright?
With no system yet with instruction,
the world will have no great misfortune.
Otherwise, all the people will face great distress.”
Xuē Shōu said:
“Do you praise it for being unlike antiquity?”
The Master said:
“In the era of Táng and Yú,
that was flourishing.
Dà Yǔ and Gāo Táo,
acted so as to obey Heaven’s good command.”
Wénzhōngzǐ said:
“Deliberation
is how the Son of Heaven gathers widely and listens broadly;
only a supremely impartial ruler can choose well.”
Wénzhōngzǐ said:
“Warnings—
are they not perfect?
The enlightened kings of old,
were cautious where they had not yet seen,
and apprehensive of what they had not yet heard;
they engraved it upon basins and goblets,
inscribed it on desks and canes;
at rest, they constantly reflected;
when active, they made no error.
Such is the merit of warning.”
Xuē Shōu said:
“Does remonstrance reveal the loyal heart of ministers?
Their intent is upright,
their words perilous.”
The Master said:
“One must be upright without being harsh,
perilous but not slanderous;
this is the way of those who understand fate.
If one is cunningly rebellious,
that is not my way.”
Jiǎ Qióng said:
How cruel,
Hàn Wǔ!
Never did he heed remonstrance.
The Master said:
Xiào Wǔ,
did he possess innate knowledge?
Though he did not comply,
he was never without pleasure in receiving remonstration.
Thus, worthy men gathered at court,
and upright words came to his ears.
This was because he was intent upon the Way,
therefore he could know regret and restore the enterprise of the empire.
Can he not be called a ruler of will?
The Master said:
The eloquence of Yáo Yì,
the wisdom of Lǐ Jìng,
the rectitude of Jiǎ Qióng and Wèi Zhēng,
the benevolence of Xuē Shōu,
the literary talent of Chéng Yuán and Wáng Xiàoyì,
combined with steadfastness,
and augmented with propriety and music,
can make a complete man.
The Master spoke of Jīng Fáng and Guō Pú,
saying they were aberrant men of old.

The Master said: When the capping ceremony is abandoned, there are no true men under heaven; when the marriage rites are neglected, there is no familial order in the world; when the funeral rites are ignored, the people become estranged from their parents; when the sacrificial rites are forgotten, the world loses memory of its ancestors. Alas! What can I do about this!
Yuè Gōng inquired about government.
The Master said:
Reverence with frugality.
Pī Gōng asked about government.
The Master said:
Purity with fairness.
Ānpíng Gōng asked about government.
The Master said:
Do not contend with others for reputation.
The Master spoke to Xuē Shōu and Jiǎ Qióng, saying:
The *Chūnqiū* and *Yuán Jīng*
express the intent of a declining age.
Their sense of righteousness and candor is faint,
their words indirect yet right.
When Yuè Gōng first met the Master,
he encountered the Grand Historian Xuē Gōng and said:
Have you seen Wáng Tōng?
Xuē Gōng replied:
He is a fellow countryman.
For seven generations his family has passed down
the art of governance,
yet none have met with favor.
Yuè Gōng said:
Can it be that for seven generations, none have met their fortune?
Xuē Gōng said:
The Way of the gentleman wanes,
and it is possible that for ten generations, none meet with success.
Yuè Gōng asked:
How is it with his ancestors?
He replied:
The Wáng family has forefathers,
and descendants as well.
Nevertheless,
enduring long in their Way,
beauty accumulates therein,
and such a person can surely set the fundamental human relations in order.
The Master departed from Pū Guān.
The official at the pass, Lù Féng, stopped him, saying:
It is not yet time to forsake my people.
The Master stayed overnight,
and left the next day.
Lù Féng escorted the Master, saying:
Go now—
the giant fishes of the rivers and lakes
cannot be contained in ditches and trenches.
Chéng Yuán said:
May I ask: Why does Wind arise from Fire in “Jiārén”?
What does it mean?
The Master said:
Clarity within and order without—
thus when the family ways are upright, so too is the world.
The Master said:
Is not benevolence and righteousness the root of teaching?
The former kings thereby continued the Way and Virtue, and elevated propriety and music.
The Master said:
Is not propriety the gate to the imperial norm?
It is that whereby the sage moves toward the light and regulates the world.
Does it not attain the Middle Way?
Therefore he can distinguish between high and low,
and settle the people’s minds.
Someone asked about the gentleman.
The Master said:
To know subtlety, to know significance,
to know gentleness, to know firmness.
He asked:
The gentleman is said to not be a vessel—
what does this mean?
The Master said:
This is what is meant by not being a vessel.
Wén Zhōngzǐ said:
In the transition between Zhōu and Qí,
the lords and high ministers had no leisure for rites.
Xiàn Gōng said:
When the Son of Heaven loses the rites,
the feudal lords rectify them within their states;
when the lords abandon the rites,
the great officers restore them in their households.
The establishment of propriety and music
was the intent of Xiàn Gōng.
Chéng Yuán asked about the aim of the Six Classics.
The Master said:
I continue the *Shū* to preserve the realities of Hàn and Jìn;
continue the *Shī* to distinguish the customs of the Six Dynasties;
revise the *Yuán Jīng* to resolve the doubts between the north and south;
commend the doctrine of the *Yì* to express the intent of former teachers;
rectify the *Lǐ* and *Yuè* to highlight the failures of later kings.
This is all there is to it.
Chéng Yuán said:
He who creates is called a sage,
he who transmits is called enlightened—
where does Master stand between these?
The Master said:
Concerning the Way,
I have only extended it again and again.
Perhaps one who delights in and finds joy in it, who labors without weariness?
How dare I claim to be sage or enlightened?
The Master said:
Some obtain by sitting,
some do not obtain by sitting;
some arrive by moving,
some do not move, yet arrive.
The Master said:
To preserve something after seeing it
is not as good as preserving it without having seen it.
The Master said:
The gentleman may be summoned, but not seduced;
may be discarded, but not insulted.
To lightly praise or blindly condemn,
to love enmity and prize anger—
such is the petty man!
The Master said:
Those who form relationships for the sake of influence—
when the influence shifts, the bond is broken;
those who form relationships for profit—
when the profit is exhausted, the bond disperses.
Therefore, the gentleman does not befriend them.
The Master said:
Xuē Shōu is skilled at dealing with petty men:
distant but not cold,
close but not overly familiar,
somewhat yielding.
The Master traveled to Fén Pavilion,
sat and played the qin.
A boatman fishing passed by
and said:
How fine,
the mood of your qin!
There is pain, yet harmony;
grievance, yet tranquility.
Dwelling in the wilds, yet possesses the ambition of court and temple.
If it is not Tài Gōng who ruled Pán Xī,
then it is Zhòngní who resided on the banks of the Sì.
The Master suddenly played “Southern Wind.”
The fisherman said:
Ha!
This is not the matter of this day.
If the Way can benefit the people,
and merit suffice to aid the world,
then do you possess the heart of the house of Yú?
It would be better to play as Shùn did himself.
The sound remains, but the mood has changed.
The Master immediately set down the qin,
and said to his disciples:
Does the transformation of feeling into sound
happen like this?
He rose to invite Yán Zhī,
but the fisherman shook his rod, beat his oar, and departed.
The disciples gave chase,
but the Master said,
"Do not pursue him."
Bō Táo Wǔ entered the river,
Jī Qìng Xiāng entered the sea—
such things are natural.
He thus committed the matter to memory
and composed "Féntíng Cāo."
The Master went to Xiàchéng,
and later, Xuē Shōu and Yáo Yì
met a swineherd and asked the way.
The herdsman asked,
"With whom are you traveling?"
Xuē Shōu said,
"With Master Wáng."
The herdsman said,
"There are birds, there are birds—
they then fly in the sky.
There are fish, there are fish—
they then dive in the deep.
Those who know the Way must remain silent."
The Master heard this,
and said to Xuē Shōu,
"Personal integrity alone suffices.
If none speak,
who will make the Way clear?"
The Master would not compare himself to others,
did not pray in sickness,
did not divine about matters contrary to right.
The Master said,
"A gentleman does not accept empty praise,
does not seek reckless fortune,
and does not avoid righteous death."
Wénzhōngzǐ said,
"Record the good in others and forget their faults—
Wēn Dàyǎ could do this.
Endure poverty and lowliness without fear—
Wèi Zhēng could do this.
Hear of one's faults and show joy—
Chéng Yuán could do this.
Be ashamed of wealth and honor in chaotic times—
Dòu Wēi could do this.
Maintain secrets without disclosure—
Dǒng Cháng could do this."
Chén Shūdá said to the Master,
"When I observe your Way,
how swift is its completion!"
The Master said,
"For one to be united with the Way and set his will on it,
what need is there to seek early achievement?"
After Shūdá went out, he met Chéng Yuán and Dòu Wēi on the road,
and spoke of it.
Chéng Yuán said,
"As for the Master’s consummation,
we have long admired the Way,
yet have never entirely satisfied our desires.
Among those who study with the Master,
there has never been one who asked and was left ignorant,
or who sought and did not receive."
The Book of Odes says:
“He has truly won my heart.”
Heaven must have inspired him;
this is not something study alone can achieve."
The Master heard this and said,
"Yuán,
do you understand?
In the world there has never been one accomplished without learning."
Someone asked about the art of long life and immortality.
The Master said,
"If humaneness and righteousness are not cultivated,
if filial piety and brotherly respect are not upheld,
why seek long life?
How boundless
is human greed!"
Someone asked about Yán Guāng and Fán Yīng, the renowned recluses.
The Master said,
"They were men who avoided discourse in ancient times."
Asked about Dōngfāng Shuò,
the Master said,
"He was one who concealed himself among men."
The Master said,
"From Tàibó and Yú Zhòng down,
few in all under Heaven have avoided the world.
Zhòngcháng Zǐguāng,
was hidden by Heaven,
and there was no place he went that was not fitting."
The Master said,
"To withdraw from the world without discontent—
is this not called evading the world?
Unless one can be wholly impartial,
he cannot be even-tempered."
Wénzhōngzǐ said,
"When the ‘Lesser Elegies’ were all neglected, the ‘Chūnqiū’ was made.
Lesser civilizing influences all declined,
and there was no longer a single emperor in the world.
"The Original Classic" was composed to continue and record,
reflecting the intent of troubled times."
The Master was in Jiàng.
Going out into the fields,
he met the governor of Chén.
He asked,
"Where are you going, Master?"
The Master said,
"I am going to Xià."
The governor of Chén ordered officials to refrain from conscription.
Dǒng Cháng, hearing of this, said,
"I understand that the Master’s travels to the states
are never in vain."
Jiǎ Qióng served the Lord of Chǔ,
but, distressed by slander, returned.
He told the Master.
The Master said,
"Qióng,
will you shut your door and sweep out all contacts?
Better to speak less and cultivate yourself within."
Qióng had not yet grasped the mind of the ancients.
Zhòngcháng Zǐguāng said,
"To scheme in danger,
is not as good as dwelling in calm and doing nothing."
Wénzhōngzǐ regarded this as wise speech.
Wénzhōngzǐ said,
"The lesser one’s name, the greater one’s virtue;
the more one withdraws, the more his Way advances.
Such a person truly understands."
The Master said,
"Those who know are not equal to those who practice;
those who practice are not equal to those who find contentment therein."
Zhòngcháng Zǐguāng’s courtesy name was Bùyào,
Dǒng Cháng’s courtesy name was Lǚcháng.
The Master said,
"Your names are virtuous."
The Master’s younger brother, Jì,
had the courtesy name Wúgōng.
The Master said,
"A courtesy name—
this is a friend’s duty.
To grant the name ‘One Without Merit’ to a sage is not appropriate for you.
Cháng gave him this name.
The youngest brother was named Jìng;
Xuē Shōu gave him the courtesy name Bǎomíng.
When the Master heard of it, he said,
"Xuē Sheng gives good courtesy names.
If Jìng is able to safeguard his reputation,
he has words of praise and warning.
Xuē Sheng is thus fit for friendship."

The Master said,
"After Tàixī,
those who record history nearly lapse into slander,
and so the gentleman is only praised after death."
The Lord of Chǔ rebelled,
and Jiǎ Qióng left him.
The Master said,
"Qióng may be said to have stood firm and not changed his position."
Wēn Yànbó asked about knowledge.
The Master said,
"I have no knowledge."
He asked about discernment.
The Master said,
"I have no discernment."
Yànbó said,
"Why is that so?"
The Master said,
"To investigate and consider—
is that truly it?"
Yànbó went and told Dǒng Cháng.
Cháng said,
"How profound it is!
This is how King Wén followed Heaven’s order."
The Master said:
“The Shī contains works about all under Heaven,
works about a single state,
and works of divine enlightenment.”
Wú Jìzhà said:
“Does the Xiǎoyǎ speak of the decline of Zhōu?
Does the Bīn speak of joy without excess?”
The Master said:
“Who claims that Jìzǐ understands joy?
Where is the decline in the Xiǎoyǎ?
Is it not the zenith of Zhōu?
Where is the joy in the Bīn?
Is it not diligence without complaint?”
The Master said:
“The sovereign of Great Harmony was truly mindful!”
Jiǎ Qióng said:
“Indeed, it is beautiful.”
The Master said:
“It is not yet radiant.”
Wénzhōngzǐ said:
“When the Shū was composed,
the gentleman no longer sought honors and emolument.”
Dǒng Cháng studied the Shū,
and reported to the Master, saying:
“Have Wú and Shǔ then been forgotten?”
The Master, with a sigh, replied:
“How can I, being knowledgeable, dare forget the noble wisdom of Dàhuáng Zhāoliè,
or the great hearts of Kǒngmíng and Gōngjǐn?”
Dǒng Cháng said:
“Great indeed,
Zhōngguó!
It is where the Five Emperors and Three Kings originated,
and from whence attire, ceremonies, and forms arose.”
Therefore, sages and worthies looked up in admiration.
When there is unity in Zhōngguó,
the sages and worthies affirm it.
When there is division in Zhōngguó,
the sages and worthies eliminate it, do they not?”
The Master said:
“Alas!
Apart from Zhōngguó, I dare not offer instruction.”
Dǒng Cháng said:
“In the Yuánjīng it is written ‘the Emperor Yuánwèi’—
why is this?”
The Master said:
“Chaos and separation are afflictions;
to whom could I turn?
Heaven and earth have providers;
the people have shelter;
that is my lord.
Moreover, dwelling in the realm of the former kings,
receiving the Way of the former kings,
and having acquired the people of the former kings—
how else should it be called?”
Dǒng Cháng said:
“May I ask, after Huángshǐ bestowed Wèi and made Jìn the emperor,
how was that so?”
The Master said:
“He who rules Zhōngguó
yet is not of Zhōngguó—
I have heard this is fate,
but have not dared proclaim it to others,
thus am myself wounded thereby.
He who is wounded cherishes it in his heart.”
Dǒng Cháng said: “May I ask, why did, in the end, Jìn receive the imperial title?”
The Master said:
“One respects the time,
and magnifies the matter;
thus is righteousness employed.”
The Master said:
“When Mùgōng came,
and Wáng Sù arrived,
then Yuánwèi was enlightened.”
The Master said:
“Without utmost impartiality, one cannot attain to the transmission of history.”
Shū Tián said:
“Why does the Yuánjīng record the fall of Chén while including five states?”
What is its reason?”
The Master said:
“Jiāngdōng
was formerly Zhōngguó,
where attire, rites, and music converged.
After Yǒngjiā,
Jiāngdōng became honored,
but in the end was not noble,
for it lacked worthy men.
Thus Qí, Liáng, and Chén were not united as one country.
At their fall,
the gentleman still remembered them.”
Therefore the Shū says:
“Jìn, Sòng, Qí, Liáng, and Chén perished,
and all five were returned as their states.”
This says only that their states perished.
Alas!
Has it come to this, that ritual and music of the former kings are thrown away?”
Shū Tián said:
“Jìn and Sòng have long since perished;
why are they counted among them now?
What does this mean?”
The Master said:
“They are the old preserve of culture, attire, and ritual;
the gentleman does not wish them to perish first.
Sòng once accomplished the restoration of Jìn,
and cherished the ambition to restore Zhōngguó.
He did not wish it to perish first either.
Therefore, Qí, Liáng, and Chén are included,
and returned as their states.
If they have not yet perished,
the gentleman deprives them of statehood,
saying:
‘Where are the rituals and music of Zhōngguó?’
If they have perished,
the gentleman still acknowledges their state,
saying:
’They are as the remaining people of Zhōngguó.’”
Shū Tián said:
“May I ask about their aspirations?”
Wénzhōngzǐ, moved to tears, stood up and said:
“It was the aspiration of the lord of Tóngchuān Prefecture,
which I have never dared abandon.”
“When five states perished together,
it was to mourn that the Way of the former kings had utterly collapsed.
Thus the gentleman enlarges his words
and uttermost laments their ruin,
sweeping the ground to seek renewal.
He awaited but did not reach the age of restoration,
and so grieved exceeding much.
Do you understand this?
For this reason the Yuánjīng records thus.”
Wénzhōngzǐ said:
“The rites and music of Hàn and Wèi,
in their later days are unworthy of praise.
Yet the Shū cannot be cast aside,
for close-to-ancient discussions and judgments are still preserved there.
As for decrees and royal command papers,
they are almost equivalent to the canonical instructions of antiquity.”
Xuē Shōu inquired about benevolence.
The Master said:
“It is the beginning of the Five Constants.”
He inquired about human nature.
The Master said:
“It is the root of the Five Constants.”
He inquired about the Way.
The Master said:
“The Five Constants are one.”
Jiǎ Qióng said:
“Master, is there something in the Way that you have not fully comprehended?”
The Master said:
“That I am not fully attuned to the Three Powers and Five Constants
is because I have been struck by the numinous spirits.
If one’s strength is insufficient,
then he ceases.”
Péi Xī asked about the affairs of Mùgōng.
The Master said:
“Have you, my uncle, not heard of the phoenix?
It views the radiance of virtue before descending;
why, then, long for what is distant?”
Shū Tián said:
“As for the affairs of Mùgōng,
they manifest the enlightenment of Qí and Wèi.”
Péi Xī said:
“What span has human life?
I look to Zhòngní,
how tireless he was!”
The Master said:
“There have been such as he.
His toiling—
who would dare oppose Heaven?
How do you know that later generations, looking upon the present,
will not regard it as we now regard the past?”
Wēn Dàyǎ asked how one may be fit to govern.
The Master said:
“Act with benevolence,
reside with tolerance,
and deeply understand the true sentiments of ritual and music.”
May I ask about the next best?
The Master said:
“In speech, be always loyal;
in action, always considerate;
unmoved by the drums of profit and harm.”
Again he asked about what comes next.
The Master said:
To be cautious and resolute,
upright and thoughtful,
to painstakingly preserve oneself,
is not enough to inspire others.
The Master said:
Descending below this,
is merely to become a wall-climber or burglar,
how could such a one be spoken of in relation to governance?
Yet such a one may be used to fill a post.
The Master said:
When clan ancestors are neglected, surnames fall apart;
when friendships are abandoned, given names are thrown into chaos.
Nèi Shǐ Xuē Gōng said to the Master:
My prose can be called excessive and indulgent.
Wénzhōngzǐ rose from his seat and bowed, saying:
I dare to congratulate the elder on knowing his own faults.
Xuē Gōng then took the Master's hand, sighed deeply, and chanted:
What hope has this old man?
This gentleman will restore the sagging net.
The Master was about to go to Xiá.
His disciples followed,
their presence resounding on the road.
The Master stopped them, saying:
Disperse.
Those who do not know me
will wonder what I seek.
The disciples then withdrew.
The Master said to Hèruò Bì:
Robust in the toes, and that's all.
The Master said:
Never has anything under Heaven been accomplished without toil.
Jiǎ Qióng asked about the way to regulate a household.
The Master said:
Let words have substance and conduct have constancy.
Wáng Xiàoyì said to the Master:
Why not speak openly?
The Master said:
Alas!
It has been long since my words have been trusted.
I will rectify the great man to obtain good fortune.
To cling to talk alone brings distress.
Moreover, to fulfill destiny and pursue one’s aspirations—
is this not the way of the gentleman?
Wénzhōngzǐ said:
Does the Chūnqiū end with Heaven’s way?
Thus it stops at the capture of the unicorn.
Does the Yuánjīng end with human affairs,
thus stopping at the fall of Chén?
In this way, Heaven and Man are both made complete.
Xuē Shōu said:
What does this mean?
The Master said:
The juncture of Heaven and Man
is greatly to be feared,
thus the gentleman is prepared for it.
The Master said:
There are those with whom one may share joy,
but not yet share sorrow;
there are those with whom one may share sorrow,
but not yet share joy.
I have never seen one with whom sorrow and joy may both be shared.
The Two Emperors and Three Kings
may be shared in sorrow.
The Master said:
If not a gentleman, one cannot discuss change with him.
The Master praised the Yì,
and upon reaching “Gé,”
he sighed, saying:
It is fit indeed—
who can accomplish this?
At “Initial Nine,”
he said:
I must be such,
but where can I act?
Xuē Shōu asked about the meaning of the six lines within one hexagram.
The Master said:
The hexagram
manifests the timing of things under Heaven;
the lines
display the movements within the world.
In adapting to the times there are six movements:
the reasons for auspiciousness, calamity, regret, and trouble being different.
Shōu said:
May I ask about the meaning of the six lines?
The Master said:
The six are no other than
the way of the Three Powers—
who can surpass it?
Chéng Yuán and Xuē Shōu met the Master.
The Master said:
In your studies of literature, what is your aim?
They replied:
The Canon of Nífù,
and your continuation of it,
we dare not be negligent.
The Master said:
Truly so, a gentleman
extends greatly and accomplishes.
At rest, he is at peace;
in action, he adapts;
such a one may assist the King.
At the funeral of Dǒng Cháng,
the Master traveled to Luò,
passing by Miǎnchí.
The host did not provide lodging,
and the Master showed signs of hunger,
sitting among thorns and brambles,
yet ceaselessly praising the Yì.
He said to his disciples:
It has been long,
I will now cease,
but having yet not received,
I do not know, though today I have thoroughly experienced great adversity.
In hardship without worry,
in poverty without fear—
the accomplished are able thus.
This is the power of study.
The host, upon hearing this,
summoned him to a proper lodging and provided a meal.
Jiǎ Qióng requested to sever human affairs.
The Master said:
It cannot be.
He requested to engage only in human affairs.
The Master said:
It cannot be.
Qióng said:
How, then, should it be?
The Master said:
Await others with dignity,
respond to them with sincerity.
Do not pursue those who depart,
do not reject those who come—
being open and easy.
Thus it is sufficient.
Wénzhōngzǐ said:
Jiǎ Yì died young,
Xiàowén passed away,
thus the fate of Hàn could be foreseen.
The Master said:
I have not seen one who is humble and bears resentment,
one who is arrogant and without disgrace,
one who is malicious and not exposed.
Dǒng Cháng said:
Master, on what do your “Twelve Plans” rely?
The Master said:
There is the Way of Heaven;
there is the Way of Earth;
there is the Way of Man;
these are their sources.
Dǒng Cháng said:
Alas!
The doctrine of the Three Ultimates—
to rely on it and practice it,
is that not brilliant?
The Master said:
If the “Twelve Plans” were put into effect in the era,
then the “Six Classics” would no longer need continuation.
Dǒng Cháng said:
What does this mean?
The Master said:
Looking up, I observe the patterns of Heaven;
looking down, I examine the structure of Earth;
in between, I establish the utmost of Man.
How could I have any leisure?
There are teachings not conveyed by words:
when practiced, all things rest in harmony.
Wénzhōngzǐ said:
When the world has the Way,
the sage conceals himself in it.
When the world lacks the Way,
the sage becomes apparent in it.
Dǒng Cháng said:
I wish to hear this explained.
The Master said:
“To return to unity without a trace—
is this not truly concealing it?
To rely on duality in order to accomplish—
can one avoid becoming manifest?
If there were one who would employ me,
I ought to reside at Tài Shān.”
Dǒng Cháng said:
“Would you then be used in a yielding manner?”
Does not the Yì say:
‘When the Yì is simple, the principles of Heaven and Earth are obtained’?”
Dù Yān asked about the master of the seven systems.
The Master said:
“He has great achievements.”
He asked what the way of Jiǎ Yì was like.
The Master said:
“All doubts are dispelled.”
Someone asked about Chǔ Yuán Wáng.
The Master said:
“A benevolent man.”
He asked about Héjiān Xiàn Wáng.
The Master said:
“A wise man.”
He asked about Dōngpíng Wáng Cāng.
The Master said:
“A humane man.”
He asked about Dōnghǎi Wáng Qiáng.
The Master said:
“A righteous man.”
To preserve honor to the end and glory in favor—
is this not fitting?
The Master said:
“When women participate in affairs, the Hàn order is endangered;
when high ministers share power equally, the destiny of Wèi becomes chaotic;
when the heir is not obedient, the House of Jìn falls.
This is not the will of Heaven;
people’s planning being unwholesome—
is this not the blame?”
Zhong Shuo, Scroll Seven
Ruǎn Yì, annotation
The Master, speaking of Wèi Xiàng,
said he was a true Chancellor of Hàn:
“He knows military strategy,
understands the mandates of the times,
how far removed he is!”
The Master said:
“Who says Qí Wénxuān was muddled
but favored Yáng Zūnyàn?
If one calls Xiàowén Míng bright—
I do not believe it.
If one calls Ěrzhū Róng
loyal—
I do not believe it.
If one calls Chén Sī Wáng
good at yielding,
and able to sully his traces,
he may be said to have moved far from penalties and reputation.
If people say he was not discreet,
I do not believe it.”
Dǒng Cháng asked:
“Of old, to be illumined without seeing,
to be keen without hearing—
was there such a thing?”
The Master said:
“Furthermore, there were those who were round but not alike,
square but not impeding,
straight but not obstinate,
curved but not cunning.”
Cháng said:
“Turbid but not foul,
clear but not dazzling,
firm but harmonious,
gentle but resolute—
is this permissible?”
The Master said:
“To go forth without making a sound,
to hide without disappearing,
to be used and thus accomplish,
to be set aside and thus remain whole—
such is between you and me.”
The Master traveled to the valley of Mǎ Jiá,
and then reached the stream at Niú Shǒu.
Ascending and descending for several nights,
his followers rejoiced.
Yáo Yì and Dòu Wēi advanced and said:
“Has the Master at last found a way to withdraw?”
The Master said:
“Though withdrawal means hiding,
it also greatly illuminates.”
Wēi said:
“I have heard the court has summoned you to deliberate.”
The Master said:
“Though they seek me, it is as if they do not get me.
If they treat me as an enemy,
neither do they overcome me.”
Yáo Yì said:
“Their carriage has already carried,
yet then they abandon your assistance.”
Dòu Wēi said:
“In the end you surpassed the peril,
which I truly did not expect.”
The Master sighed,
and then sang the “First Month” to the end.
Afterward he said:
“Nothing can be done.”
The Master said:
“The *Shū* discriminates affairs;
the *Shī* rectifies nature;
the *Lǐ* regulates conduct;
the *Yuè* harmonizes virtue;
the *Chūnqiū* and *Yuán Jīng* bring forth the past;
the *Yì* foreknows what is to come.
The treasury of the former kings is thoroughly exhausted.”
Wáng Xiàoyì said:
“Alas! The Master does not serve;
a wise man is born in vain.”
Jiǎ Qióng said:
“Is the Master merely born in vain?
He takes the ten thousand ages as his models,
the five constants as his four quarters,
the three talents and nine categories as his counselors and ministers—
what need is there to serve?”
Dǒng Cháng said:
“The Master takes the Continued *Shī* and Continued *Shū* as his court,
the Discourses on *Lǐ* and *Yuè* as his administration,
the Commentary on the *Yì* as his Office of Fate,
the *Yuán Jīng* as his rewards and punishments.
This is the way in which the Master lives.”
Shū Tián, hearing this, said:
“Filial piety and brotherly deference are the altars of state;
silence is the ancestral temple;
to know all things is wealth and honor;
to bring all things to completion is life and death.
All under Heaven pay reverence to him;
the Master's way is complete.”
Jiǎ Qióng said:
“Wú Qīn of Zhōngshān
is the most filial of all under Heaven.
When at home,
his father and elder brothers are pleased;
when conducting affairs,
his father and elder brothers grow anxious,
as if they had nothing to rely upon.”
The Master said:
“The filial among my associates are different:
When at home,
parents are serene;
when conducting affairs,
father and elder brothers are at ease,
as if they had nothing to worry about.”
Péi Jiā had a wedding gathering,
and Xuē Fāngshì attended.
In the midst of the wine, music was played;
Fāngshì disapproved and left.
On hearing of this, the Master said:
“Xuē Fāngshì knows propriety,
but is he still behind the gentlemen?”
Master Wénzhōng said:
“The *Yuán Jīng* has constants:
what it rectifies lies in the Way—
in this one sees righteousness.
The *Yuán Jīng* also has transformations:
what it applies to has appropriateness—
in this one sees expediency.
When expediency and righteousness are both upheld,
the Sovereign Pivot is established.”
Dǒng Cháng said:
“With the Master’s ‘Six Classics’,
the ultimate in the Sovereign Pivot’s function is achieved.”
Wén Zhōngzǐ said:
“The *Chūnqiū* [Spring and Autumn Annals]
is the chronicle of a single state.
Why, when there are many states under Heaven,
does it not revere the royal house?
Therefore it restrains the feudal lords to honor the royal government,
and clarifies that the Mandate of Heaven is not yet changed—
this is the work of the *Chūnqiū*.
The *Yuánjīng* [Primordial Classic],
is the book of all under Heaven.
Why, when there is no fixed state, is the imperial position unclear?
By examining the Mandate of Heaven, it puts the imperial position in order,
and clarifies the true destination of the sacred implements—
this is the work of the *Yuánjīng*.”
Dǒng Cháng said:
“Clinging to minor righteousness hinders great authority;
is this not what the *Chūnqiū* and *Yuánjīng* condemn?”
The Master said:
“This is called the Emperor’s failing to reach the utmost.”
At the Yuhe campaign,
the Master heard of it and said:
“The strength of the people is exhausted.”
When the Master was at home,
he never for a moment set aside the *Zhouli* [Rites of Zhōu].
His disciples asked him.
The Master said:
“The Former Master took the Way of Kingship as the highest.
If anyone employs me,
I would hold to this and go forth.”
Tōng was a descendant of the royal house of Zhōu;
how would he dare to forget its rites?”
The Master said:
“Does the *Zhouli* oppose the Mandate of Heaven?
The *Chūnqiū*,
by elevating Lǔ over the King,
does it follow what remains of Zhōu?
The *Yuánjīng* sets the Son of Heaven above the Emperor and honors Zhongguó;
is it because the Mandate of Heaven has found its place?”
Zhāng Xuánsù asked about rites.
The Master said:
“Make your heart upright,
compose your bearing with dignity,
act with thoughtfulness and respect,
be still with thoughts of rectitude.”
He asked about the Way.
The Master said:
“When you obtain rites, the Way endures.”
After Xuánsù withdrew,
the Master said:
“He has a heart for ritual.
Some attain a name by stealing from the rites—
how much more by diligent practice!”
Wèi Zhēng asked about the disputation of the gentleman.
The Master said:
“What need is there for the gentleman to be disputatious?
If there is a time when he must dispute,
it is from necessity,
is it not like the use of arms?”
Dǒng Cháng, hearing this, said:
“A gentleman has arguments that need no words,
weapons that do not slay,
is there a time for that as well?”
The Master said:
“Truly!
Not knowing the proper time,
one is incapable of being a gentleman.”
Wén Zhōngzǐ said:
“He who, on hearing slander, becomes angry—
this is the opening for flattery.
He who, on hearing praise, feels joy—
this is the medium for sycophancy.
Cut off the opening and remove the medium,
and calumny and flattery will be far from you.”
The Master said:
“On hearing difficulties, think of how to resolve;
on seeing gain, think of avoiding it;
take pleasure in completing others’ virtue—
thus you can establish yourself.”
The Master said to Dǒng Cháng:
“I have yet to see one who is diligent.
Perhaps such a one exists—
but I have not seen him.”
The Master said:
“If the years do not yield abundance,
and war does not cease,
what can I do?”
The Master said that Huáng Gōng of Běishān excelled at medicine—
he put rest and food before needles and drugs;
Hóu Shēng of Fényīn excelled at divination—
he put human matters before reading the trigrams.
Fáng Xuánlíng asked about the way the ruler’s rectitude shelters the people.
The Master said:
“First, forget oneself.”
He said:
“Pray, explain this in detail.”
The Master said:
“Only those who can forget themselves
are able to be free from selfishness;
only by being free from selfishness
can one achieve utmost impartiality;
only then can one take all under Heaven as his charge,
and the Way can be realized.”
Xuánlíng said:
The Master said:
“If one is truly thorough, explanation is not needed.
Even Xiāo and Zhāng seem to have fallen short.
Alas!
It is not something you can reach.
Just hold fast to your reverence,
grasp your caution,
and you will be able to serve people.”
There was disorder in Jiāngdū,
and the Master was ill.
He said to Xuē Shōu:
“The Way has long been neglected.
If a true king were to arise,
it would take thirty years before the rites and music could be spoken of as accomplished—
that is all.”
Shōu said:
“What do you mean by this?”
The Master said:
“Ten years to bring peace,
ten years to bring prosperity,
ten years to harmonize—
then it shall be accomplished.”
The Master said:
“Marriage at an early age, with bride-prices too low—
this inculcates idleness.
Un-numbered concubines and secondary wives—
this inculcates disorder.
Moreover, difference in social status is only right;
one husband and one wife—
that is the duty of the common people.”
The Master paid respects to the Sui founder,
and after one meeting presented the *Twelve Strategies*,
editing them into four volumes.
Xuē Shōu said:
“How eloquent!”
Dǒng Cháng said:
“It is not eloquence,
but principle that makes it so.”
Fáng Xuánlíng asked to study the *Twelve Strategies*.
The Master said:
“Times change and circumstances alter;
there is no need to study them.”
Yú Shìjī sent an envoy saying to the Master:
“Why not enter official service?”
The Master said:
“Tōng (I) am unwell
and cannot serve.”
He feasted the envoy
and sang the ‘Lesser Brightness’ to send him off.
When Shìjī heard this, he said:
“I am but lingering in the world of netted silk;
as for the Master—he is of a secret surpassing depth.”
Wén Zhōngzǐ said:
“When asked, I answer;
when not asked, I set forth;
some compare me to Dōng Zhòngshū.”
The Master said:
“ Because I did not enter office,
I completed my achievement;
because I did not act rashly,
I have no regret;
because I did not seek extensively,
I have attained;
because I did not pursue miscellaneous studies,
I have clarity.”
Wén Zhōngzǐ said:
“Sluggishness
is the canker of wisdom;
resentment and hatred
are the bane of benevolence;
pettiness and stinginess
are the rot of righteousness.”
The Master said:
“The exclusive judgments of the Yuánjīng—
these are concealed within Heaven’s Mandate.
How could I dare to reach such heights?”
Dǒng Cháng, having heard this, said:
“Regarding the Yuánjīng and Heaven’s Mandate,
if you, Master, do not attain them,
who else could possibly attain them?”
The Master said to Dòu Wēi:
“Upon capping, read the ‘Rites of Capping’;
when about to marry, read the ‘Rites of Marriage’;
in mourning, read the ‘Rites of Mourning’;
after the funeral, read the ‘Rites of Sacrifice.’
At court, read the ‘Rites of Guests’;
on military campaigns, read the ‘Rites of the Army.’
Thus, the gentleman never departs from the Rites all his life.”
Dòu Wēi said:
“Zhòngní said:
‘Without studying the Rites,
one cannot stand.’
Is this what is meant?”
The Master expounded on the ‘Rites of Marriage.’
Jiǎ Qióng said:
“Now all these have been lost;
how then can they be continued?”
The Master said:
“Qióng,
do not belittle the Rites,
do not flatter vulgar customs;
it is enough to preserve them for now.”
The Master praised the Yì, reaching the Guān Hexagram,
saying:
“With this, one may exhaust the spirits.”
The Master said:
“In ancient times, the worthy were promoted and the unworthy demoted,
yet still there was anxiety over misgovernment.
Now I rejoice for the worthy and pity the unworthy;
in this way, one incurs few resentments,
and even so I fear not to be spared.”
The Shī says:
“Trembling and fearful at heart,
as if facing a hollow valley.”
The Master read the Shuōyuǎn.
He said:
“This may be used to aid teaching.”
When the Master went to Hánchéng,
he crossed through Lóngménguān ahead;
Jiǎ Qióng and Chéng Yuán followed after.
The customs officer, Chóu Zhāng, stopped him, saying:
“Who is it that crossed first?
I see his brow droops as if yielding,
serene but not dull;
his eyes glitter as if shining,
clear and unblinking;
his mouth is honest as if forthright,
broad but not boastful;
he has a phoenix’s neck and a turtle’s back,
his beard hangs to his waist,
long as if trailing.
When walking with him,
he stoops and his appearance is humble;
when speaking with him,
he responds slowly and after reflection.
Though the waves startled him and swept him around, he was unafraid.
Surely this must be someone remarkable.
I have heard:
When the world is without the Way,
the sage hides away—
bowed and silent, guarding stillness;
this man is perhaps like that.”
Chéng Yuán said:
“Master, you can recognize people truly.
That is Wáng Tōng.”
Jiǎ Qióng said:
“The two of us have taken him as our teacher, but cannot leave him.”
Chóu Zhāng said:
“Supporting himself on a single virtue,
riding the Five Constants,
upholding the Three Powers,
mastering the Six Arts—
how could I stay behind and not follow?”
So he left his post and followed to Hánchéng.
The Master said to Jiǎ Qióng:
“A true gentleman,
this Chóu Zhāng!
Compared with Dǒng Cháng he is not sufficient,
but beside Xuē Shōu, he has more than enough.”
Wén Zhōngzǐ said:
“I have heard of rites from Guān Shēng,
and observed their traces in a woodcutter bearing a load;
authentic music from Huò Shēng,
and saw its traces in a man holding a rod.
So I shall withdraw and seek them among the fields and wilds.”
The Master said:
“One who talks much cannot be counted on for distant plans;
one who acts much cannot be relied upon for long companionship.
I would like to meet someone who is false in calm and feigned in frugality.”
Jiǎ Qióng said:
“To know what is good and not do it,
to see what is right but not encourage it,
even if welcomed by jade discs held in both hands,
I would not enter such a man’s gate.”
When the Master heard this, he said:
“How resolutely upright!”
Chóu Zhāng said to Xuē Shōu:
“Have you heard of the Three Haves and the Seven Have-nots?”
Shōu said:
“What are they?”
Zhāng said:
“No rash assent,
no wealth to breed resentments,
no monopolizing profits,
no insincere talk,
no boasting of goodness,
no casting aside of others,
no harboring of grudges.”
Xuē Shōu said:
“May I hear the Three Haves?”
Zhāng said:
“Have benevolence,
have frugality,
and do not place oneself before all under Heaven.”
Shōu said:
“Do you possess these?”
He replied:
“These are the duties of the gentleman;
how should Zhāng presume to claim them?”
When the Master heard this, he said:
“Precisely because he has them,
he so resembles the true one.”
The Master said:
“A gentleman first selects, then befriends;
a petty man first befriends, then selects.
Therefore, the gentleman has few faults;
the petty man has many grievances.
Is this not the reason?”
The Master said:
“A gentleman does not demand what people cannot reach,
does not force people to do what they cannot,
does not make things hard for people regarding what they do not like.
Thus,
he is spared from blame.”
Lǎo Dān said:
“My words are very easy to practice,
yet under Heaven none can practice them.
Truly!”
Chóu Zhāng asked:
“Does the gentleman contend?”
The Master said:
“When seeing profit, he contends to yield it;
hearing of rightness, he contends to enact it;
where there is wrong, he contends to change it.”
Xuē Shōu asked:
“How are the sage and Heaven and Earth related?”
The Master said:
“Heaven gives birth,
Earth nourishes,
the sage completes.
Therefore, with Heaven and Earth established, the Yì is enacted among them.”
Xuē Shōu asked about the Yì.
The Master said:
“The center of Heaven and Earth is nothing else
but man.”
Shōu withdrew sighing, saying:
“It is only now that I know—if human affairs are cultivated,
then the principles of Heaven and Earth are attained.”
The Master said to Shōu:
“I have never seen one who desired benevolence and loved righteousness and yet could not obtain them.
If one does not obtain them,
then perhaps he has no true nature.”
The Master said:
“Yán Zǐlíng fished at Tuānshí,
Ěr Zhū Róng strove to dominate under Heaven.
Therefore, the gentleman does not value gaining office highly.”
The Master said:
“Fire blazes upward but is subdued by water;
water flows downward but attains its aim over fire.
Therefore, the gentleman does not wish to constantly rise above others.”
The Master praised the Yì, saying that when the mountain is pressed to the earth and is eroded away,
he said:
“It stands firm in its place.
Where shall it go for safety?
Therefore the junzi thinks of humbling himself below others.”
When Ruìchéng Fǔjūn was reading the Shuōyuàn,
the Master saw him and said:
“Excellent,
such is your aspiration, elder brother!
In using this to further things,
is it not fitting?
In your dwelling,
you are always serene as water.
In speech, always forgiving;
in action, always righteous;
you deal with others sincerely, awaiting the right occasion.
Therefore, the junzi delights in his way,
while the petty man cherishes its benefits.”
Shū Tián said:
“In adhering to the way of the former kings,
I act with reflection and recite while sitting,
always as if I am not measuring up;
in facing affairs and dealings,
always as if I have not been instructed;
truly, the Way is difficult!”
The Master said:
“So am I.”
Shū Tián said:
“The world hates straightforwardness and detests uprightness;
are you alone able to be at peace in it?”
The Master, somewhat despondent, changed his expression and said:
“Let the spirits listen to this.
May you receive magnificent blessings.
As for the junzi and his Way,
he ceases only in death.
Heaven does not halt the cycles of cold and heat because of people’s grievances,
nor does the junzi cease being upright because of others’ wickedness.
But have you not heard the words of the Hóngfàn?
‘Level, peaceful, upright, and correct.’
Thus,
integrity is preserved.
Now you are fussy and anxious,
the three virtues lack a foundation,
and your heart has not been steadfast.
No boldness,
no frankness,
no firmness,
no resistance—
this is called crookedness and deviance.
The people act with excess and error;
might it not be because of you?
Shū Tián bowed twice and withdrew.
Qiú Zhāng stepped forward and said:
“The junzi thinks of humbling himself below others;
is this to be found only in this?”
The Master smiled but did not reply.
Xuē Shōu said:
“The junzi laughs only when genuinely joyful.
Master, why did you not accept his advancement?”
The Master said:
“Only the passionate can master reflection—
is this not joy?”
The Master said to Qiú Zhāng and Xuē Shōu:
“It is not that knowledge is difficult;
acting on it is what is truly difficult.”
Ruǎn Yì’s commentary
Wénzhōngzǐ said:
“When fate is established,
can it be called human affairs?
Therefore the junzi is in awe of it.
There is nothing far or near, high or deep, that does not respond to it;
nothing great or small, bent or straight, that does not suit it.
Thus, it is attributed to Heaven.
The Yì says:
‘The Way of Qián transforms and creates,
each keeps to its own nature and destiny.’”
Wèi Zhēng said:
“The Shū says:
‘Go along with kindness and there is fortune;
follow resistance and there is harm;
just like sound and echo.’
The Shī says:
‘Not being restrained, not being troubled;
receiving blessings without limit.
In such friendship there is no arrogance;
all blessings come seeking it out.’
Is this not what is meant?”
The Master said:
“Zhēng is capable of seeking it for himself.”
Dǒng Cháng said:
“Is what is ‘self-sought’ called human action?”
The Master said:
“Truly so!
It is only what a person summons for himself.”
Jiǎ Qióng stepped forward and said:
“May I ask—
‘Life and death are decreed by fate,
wealth and rank lie with Heaven’—
what does this mean?”
The Master said:
“What is summoned comes first;
what is fated comes after;
this is what is called self-seeking.
Yet is this not also fate?
Alas!
There is nothing more I can say.”
Qióng bowed and withdrew,
and said to Chéng Yuán:
“Only now do I understand that the ‘original Mandate’ may be established,
and much blessing may be sought.”
Chéng Yuán said:
“I revere and admire the Master’s words,
and I will hold to them without tire.”
Wénzhōngzǐ said:
“To measure virtue and then take a teacher;
to exchange sons and thus instruct each other—
now, these have perished.”
The Master said:
“One who does not use the way of Yī Yǐn and Zhōu Gōng to strengthen his state
is not a great minister;
one who does not serve his lord with the loyal intent of Huò Guāng and Zhūgě Liàng
is merely a routine subject.”
Dǒng Cháng sighed and said:
“How admirable
is the heart of Yánzǐ!
For three months he did not depart from benevolence.”
The Master heard this and said:
“Benevolence is not far away;
just reflect carefully and practice it,
and do not crave after it lightly.
Only by being pure and single-minded
will you first ascend to the shore.”
Cháng withdrew and said:
“Reflection not reaching to purity,
thought not arriving at wisdom—
how can one be without faults?
How can one not fall short?”
Fán Shīxuán heard that Dǒng Cháng was virtuous,
and asked Jiǎ Qióng about his age.
Qióng said:
“He has just come of age.”
Shīxuán said:
“Ah! He is precociously wise.”
Qióng said:
“The Master became a teacher at fifteen.
Wáng Xiàoyì of Chénliú,
who was proud among his predecessors,
yet with white hair he faced him as a disciple.
Was it because of age?”
Qióng heard this:
“Virtue is not in years;
the Way is not in position.”
Among the disciples, someone asked Yáo Yì:
“At the gate of Kǒng’s court, why are only the Shī and Lǐ
spoken of,
but not the four classics?”
Why is this?”
Yáo Yì said:
“I have heard it from the Master:
The Chūnqiū severs things, after intention is settled, one can reach it;
Lè brings harmony, after virtue is whole, one can reach it;
the Shū sets rules and laws, after serving in office, one can reach it;
the Yì exhausts principles, after knowing fate, one can reach it.
Thus, if you do not study the Chūnqiū,
you will not be able to master judgment;
if you do not study the Lè, you will not understand harmony;
if you do not study the Shū, you will not be able to discuss standards;
if you do not study the Yì,
you will not be able to penetrate principle.
Without the physical capacity for all four,
one cannot reach them.
Therefore, the sage ranked them last.
Could they be basic tools for nurturing the untutored?”
Someone said:
“If so, why are the Shī and the Lǐ taught first?”
Yì answered:
“When one is taught with the Shī,
their words and tone become refined,
and thus they are far removed from ferocity or insolence.
Restraining them with the Lǐ,
their gestures and appearance become orderly,
thus establishing dignity and respect.
Measure their words,
examine their intentions,
assess their conduct,
distinguish their virtue.
Once the will is settled, express it through the Chūnqiū,
thus making one resolute yet able to adapt;
once virtue is complete, guide with music,
thus bringing harmony and a sense of moderation;
when ready for action,
convey it through the Shū,
thus enabling one to establish regulations;
understanding destiny, expand with the Yì,
thus one may exhaust the potential of their nature.
If suddenly one is instructed in the Chūnqiū,
then their resolve will be unsettled and sense of righteousness light;
if suddenly in music,
then their virtue will be disturbed and their measure corrupted;
if suddenly in the Shū,
then they will treat laws with too much familiarity;
if suddenly in the Yì,
then they will trifle with the divine.
For this reason, the sage knows this is inevitable,
thus he establishes it with a foundation,
and arranges it in sequence.
First perfect oneself,
then extend it to things;
first achieve what is near,
then manifest what is distant.
How profound it is!
How profound it is!
Zǐ, hearing this, said:
“Yáo Yì has attained it.”
Zǐ said:
“When knowledge is lesser than insight,
when virtue is lighter than talent,
that is error indeed.”
Zǐ said:
“Order and disorder—these follow the cycles,
some take advantage of them,
some reform them.
Success and failure are a matter of timing,
some go forth in them,
some encounter them.
Auspiciousness and calamity—this is destiny,
some create them,
some receive them by coincidence.
Coming and going in turn,
each arrives by its own reckoning—
how could these be spoken of idly?”
“In the campaign of Liáodōng,
the whole world built ships.”
Zǐ said:
“The forests and hills are exhausted.
When the Emperor inspects his mountains,
with what words will he reply?”
Someone asked about the Xù Jīng.
Xuē Shōu and Yáo Yì reported to Zǐ.
He said:
“If the worthy criticize,
I will respond with adorned sincerity;
if the foolish criticize,
how will I answer them alone?”
So he recited the final stanza of “Shǔlí”
and upon entering, said to his disciples:
“Five alliances, three betrayals—
Liú Jùn truly understands words!”
Fáng Xuánlíng asked:
“When praising goodness, ascribe it to your lord;
when acknowledging faults, take them on oneself—is this loyalty?”
Zǐ said:
“It is yielding.”
Dù Rúhuì asked about governance.
Zǐ said:
“Extend your sincerity,
promote your kind;
reward one to encourage a hundred,
punish one to warn the multitude.
What difficulty is there in governing thus?”
After Rúhuì left,
he said to Dòu Wēi:
“The upright permit frankness;
the fawning block gradual criticism;
reward and punishment lie within these.
Do I not now understand governance?”
Wén Zhōng Zǐ said:
“Legislation did not match the time of Huáng Chū;
intention and affairs did not match the era of Tài Xī;
praise and blame did not match the period of Rén Shòu.”
Shū Tián said:
“What do you mean?”
Zǐ, with tears, said:
“Between Rén Shòu and Dà Yè,
can one even bear to speak of what happened?”
Jiǎ Qióng asked:
“To enrich and then teach—
what does this mean?”
Zǐ said:
“Benevolence arises from want;
righteousness arises from abundance.
Therefore to enrich and then teach
is easy.
In ancient times the sage kings were above;
fields and hamlets were distant;
the calls of chickens and dogs could be heard from afar;
yet people grew old and died without visiting one another—
for they were self-sufficient.”
“Thus, in an era of perfect order,
the five codes remained latent,
the five rituals were set aside,
the five mourning garments were not clearly distinguished.
People knew how to eat and drink,
but not how to store their harvest;
they knew to live together,
but not how to love and respect each other.
Those above were like trees waving in the wind;
those below were like deer on the plains.
Why was this so?
Because those above did not interfere,
and those below were self-sufficient.”
Jiǎ Qióng said:
“When purity is diluted and simplicity dissolves,
can it ever be regained?”
Zǐ said:
“Humans can broaden the Way;
if one attains the proper conduct,
it is as easy as turning a hand.
In the past, Shùn and Yǔ succeeded one another and the world was simple;
Jié of Xià inherited it and the world became deceitful;
Chéng Tāng overthrew Jié and the world was at peace;
Zhòu of Yīn inherited and the world declined;
Wén and Wǔ governed and Yōu and Lì were scattered;
Wén and Jǐng brought peace, but Huán and Líng were lost.
Thus, order and chaos succeed one another;
culture and corruption have their reasons.
Rise and decline depend on the people;
gain and loss lie in teaching.
To claim that the highest antiquity cannot return
is not to know the transforming power of the former kings.
If so, why the Shī, Shū, Lǐ, and Yuè?
Dǒng Cháng, having heard this,
said to Jiǎ Qióng:
“If the teachings of Kǒngzǐ and Mèngzǐ were lost,
but Master’s Way was practiced,
then what is meant by ‘rest and they will come, set in motion and they will harmonize’?
Who says simplicity and honesty cannot return?”
Zǐ said:
“Few indeed can master the passions with their nature.
I have never seen a person facing a crossroads without hesitation.
The Yì says:
‘Direct, upright, and great—
unpracticed,
nothing is unfavorable.’
This is to act without doubt.”
Dòu Wēi said:
“How great is the Yì’s fulfillment of nature!
Which disciple has reached it?”
Zǐ said:
“Dǒng Cháng is close to it.”
Someone asked:
“How do Wēi and Cháng compare?”
Zǐ said:
“I do not know.”
Zǐ said:
“The Dà Yǎ nearly approaches the Way;
truly, it is for the hidden ones.
Working in silence and accomplishing,
not speaking and yet inspiring trust.”
Someone asked about Táo Yuánliàng.
The Master said:
He was a man who cast himself away.
"Return Home" contains the intent to withdraw from the world.
"Biography of Master Wǔliǔ"
is already close to shutting himself away.
The Master said:
To reconcile great enmity always leaves some resentment;
to forget great joy always leaves some joy.
Such is the Way of Heaven.
The Master said:
Qì ranks above;
form is below;
consciousness resides in between;
thus the Three Powers are complete.
Qì is ghostly;
is it not of Heaven?
Consciousness is spirit;
is it not human?
I obtain these from reason and nature.
Xuē Shōu said:
May I ask, regarding Heaven, spirit, man, and ghost,
what do they mean?
Was Zhōu Gōng able to understand?
The Master said:
How great
was Zhōu Gōng!
To probe the distant is to fathom it with the mind.
The mind is nothing else
but the investigator of principle.
Therefore, all is rooted in Heaven.
To attribute spirit to Heaven
is to revere and distance it.
Thus sacrificial rites are employed to communicate.
To seek the near is to search within oneself.
The self is none other
than the one who exhausts his nature.
In the end, all reverts to man.
To attribute ghosts to men
is to bring them close and respect them.
Thus feasting rites are used to communicate.
In antiquity, observing the cleansing but not presenting offerings
was already to have thought more than half.
Xuē Shōu said:
May I ask about the Earth spirits?
The Master said:
It is profound indeed!
All things are born there,
the myriad kinds take form there.
Manifested to the people—
this is its meaning.
Form
is nothing else
but what is called bone and flesh.
Thus sacrificial rites are used to communicate.
Shōu said:
Which of the three comes first?
The Master said:
The Three Powers do not exist apart.
In application to enterprise,
one assumes primacy.
The round altar honors sacrifice,
to observe the Way of spirits;
the square pond esteems offerings,
to examine the categories of things;
the ancestral temple uses feasting,
to cherish essence and qì.
Shōu said: May I ask about the profundities of the Three Powers?
The Master said:
How profound the question!
Heaven
collects the primordial qì;
it is not merely the vast expanse of blue;
Earth
collects the primordial form;
it is not merely the mountains and rivers;
Man
collects the primordial consciousness;
it is not merely round head and square feet.
The profundities of Qián and Kūn—
have you considered them?
Thereupon, Shōu withdrew to study the Yì.
The Master said:
Archery was used to observe virtue,
but now it is lost.
The ancients honored benevolence and righteousness,
and set little value on courage and strength.
The Master said:
To discard virtue and betray righteousness,
yet lament that people do not draw near;
to delight in suspicion and value deceit,
yet grieve that people do not trust;
thus it always has been.
The Master said:
The gentleman wins people's hearts,
not just their words;
those who win only words,
do not win men's persons.
To win men's persons
is only by force.
The gentleman uses righteousness;
the petty man uses force.
How difficult indeed!
The Master said:
After Tài Xī,
the Son of Heaven only retained the title.
Alas!
To impose moral transformation by policy
is to make vassals equal to him.
Why does the "Yuan Jing" fail to flourish?
Fáng Xuánlíng said to Xuē Shōu:
That the Way is not practiced is inevitable;
why, Master, do you labor so vigorously?
Xuē Shōu said:
Are you not a disciple of the Master?
If the Son of Heaven loses the Way,
then the feudal lords should cultivate it;
if the feudal lords lose the Way,
then the great officers should cultivate it;
if the great officers lose the Way,
then the scholars cultivate it;
if the scholars lose the Way,
then the common people cultivate it.
Thus the way of cultivation
looks to teachers wherever they may be,
teaching tirelessly,
exhausted yet not reckless,
ceasing only at death.
When the time is right, then act;
when the time is wrong, then hide away.
Thus is the Way of the Former Kings transmitted without end,
the ancients called it "continuing the times."
Does not the Classic of Poetry say:
Though I do not go,
will you not continue the sound?
Why then should the practice cease merely because none follow it?
Xuánlíng, startled, bowed and said:
Can its practice be so far-reaching?
"Central Sayings," scroll nine
Ruǎn Yì, commentary
Someone asked about Guān Lǎng.
The Master said:
He was a worthy man of Wèi.
When Emperor Xiàowén died and Xuānwǔ succeeded,
Lord Mù died,
Guān Lǎng withdrew.
The decline of Wèi has its cause!
The Master said:
When the Central States lose the Way,
the Four Barbarians know of it.
Wèi Zhēng said:
May I hear your views?
The Master said:
When the "Lesser Odes" are utterly discarded,
and the Four Barbarians invade in turns,
this is when the Central States have lost the Way;
is this not so?
Zhēng withdrew and said to Xuē Shōu:
The times can thus be known.
Xuē Shōu asked:
Why do people nowadays have no poetry?
The Master said:
Poetry
is the true feelings and nature of the people.
Can true feelings and nature perish?
It is not that the people have no poetry,
the blame lies with those whose duty is poetry.
Yáo Yì was beset by poverty.
Fáng Xuánlíng said,
“Alas,
such poverty!
Why not ask for help?”
Yáo Yì replied,
“In ancient times, when someone asked for others’ sake,
even that was considered yielding or being deferential with residence;
how much more so when asking for oneself?
I do not wish to do so.”
The Master heard this and said,
“How resolute, such righteousness!
Truly he carries out the Way of the ancients;
this teaches me something:
it is hard to advance, yet easy to retreat.”
The Master said,
“Even in what is near at hand, there must be something to be examined;
but if one seeks the root, it lies far off.”
Wáng Guī’s cousin sought the Xù Jīng.
The Master said, “Uncle,
by what virtue are you suited to receive it?”
Guī said,
“Do not decline.
To accept responsibility, one must not yield even to a teacher;
how much more when there is no teacher?
I have heard Guān Lǎng’s divination:
after great turmoil,
a great sage must arise.
Of those well-versed in the Rites and the Music,
none surpasses our clan.
Heaven has not abandoned the Way;
as for those who will revive true learning,
if not you, who else?”
Wèi Zhēng asked,
“What of governing affairs by policy deliberation and statutory codes?”
The Master said,
“If one first rectifies the fundamental,
punishments will be laid to rest.
If the Way is lost,
what benefit in policy deliberation?
Therefore, in the era of perfect governance,
laws hang yet go unviolated;
the next best is that, though violated, they are not numerous.
Thus, to deliberate policy by statutes—
alas!—this is but the method of the middle ages.
If someone were to employ me,
would there surely be no lawsuits?”
Wén Zhōngzǐ said,
“After Píng Chén,
the virtue of the dragon became excessive,
yet in the end there was no repentance.
Such sorrow!”
The Master said,
“In my work on the Xù Shū and the Yuán Jīng,
does it express awareness of Heaven’s mandate?
When mourning for the loss of rites and music, I composed chapters and treatises;
in rectifying the calendar and numbers, I defined the South and North;
moved by the imperial system, I began with Tài Xī;
exalting the Central States, I set straight the origins of the emperors.”
Wén Zhōngzǐ said,
“In action, error lies in excess;
in stillness, in lack.”
The Master said,
“No crime is greater than delighting in advancement;
no disaster is greater than excessive speech;
no pain is greater than not hearing one’s faults;
no disgrace is greater than not knowing shame.”
The Master said,
“That the son of the Son of Heaven should don the capping ceremony and discuss enfeoffment, understand governance and receive office—this is the ancient way.”
Xuē Shōu asked Zhòngcháng Zǐguāng about government.
Zǐguāng said,
“When a single main cord is raised,
all the threads are set;
if a single loom is slackened,
a myriad things collapse.
Such a one does not understand government.”
Shōu reported this to Wén Zhōngzǐ.
The Master said,
“Zǐguāng has got it.”
Wén Zhōngzǐ said,
“Without knowing the Way,
one cannot be a minister to others,
let alone be a ruler.”
The Master said,
“If people do not dwell together,
and land is not parceled in wells,
in the end even if there is the Way,
not even Shùn or Yǔ could bring order.”
The Master said,
“If government is too harsh,
better to be benevolent;
if law is too swift,
better to be slow;
if litigation is too plentiful,
better to be simple;
between minister and ruler,
better to trust than to be suspicious.
Of those who hold to the mean,
who but the sage?”
The Master said,
“Delegating responsibility to more than one,
is the source of chaos;
unceasing supervision,
is the breeding ground of treachery.”
Péi Xī, hearing this, said,
“If left and right are mutually suspicious,
is this not disorder?
If higher and lower spy on each other,
is this not treachery?
In antiquity this was called the ‘government of serpents and swine.’
Alas!
This is the crime for which Qín perished.”
Dù Yán asked about withdrawal.
The Master said,
“It is not that one hides oneself away and is unseen,
but when the times and mandate are gravely out of joint, one hides one’s virtue.
Only one possessed of the Way can do this.
Therefore it is called ‘retreating and storing oneself in obscurity.’”
Dù Yán said,
“In the rise of the Yì,
can the realm truly be doubted,
thus that the sage may hide?”
The Master said,
“To show benevolence yet hide its practice:
this is the method of the middle ages.”
Yán said,
“May I ask about the doctrine of hiding?”
The Master said,
“Obliterate its traces,
let your heart shine forth;
it may be grasped spiritually,
not attained through things:
this is its doctrine.”
He further asked the import of the Way.
The Master said,
“Do not act contrary to ritual;
do not look without ritual;
do not listen without ritual.”
Yán said,
“These are the eyes of the benevolent man.”
The Master said,
“The Way lies within.”
Yán withdrew and said to Rú Huì,
“Look for it ahead,
and suddenly it is behind—
truly the Yán clan knows this.”
Wén Zhōngzǐ said,
“If the four classes are not distinguished,
the five ranks not established,
the six officials not in their posts,
the nine divisions not in order,
then the ancient tombs and canonical texts of Emperors cannot be recognized.
If one does not use the laws of the Three Dynasties to unify the realm,
the state will ultimately be in peril.
If compelled by necessity,
then employ the system of the Two Hàn.
To fail to aid the world with the system of the Two Hàn—
this is truly chaos.”
Wén Zhōngzǐ said,
“Of the transmission by Zhòng Ní,
all is vast, entire, and complete.
Though a thousand years may pass without its use,
it is deeply to be mourned!”
Qiú Zhāng stepped forward and said,
“And yet why, Master, do you so labor over your transmissions now?”
The Master said,
“It is the duty of the former sages;
I dare not abandon it.
How can we know that those after us may not use it?
If there are the tender reeds and rushes,
then there will be years of abundance.”
The Master said to Xuē Shōu:
“Yuán Wèi has already fallen;
the world is now without a ruler.
In the ninth year of Kāihuáng,
the people were first unified.
The elders had a saying:
‘Those who respect an undertaking make its beginning great;
those who are cautious in their position make their name upright.’
This is why I offered counsel at Rénshòu.
Your Majesty is a true emperor;
do not follow in the steps of false usurpers;
you must succeed Zhōu and Hàn.
Use earth to succeed fire,
honor the color yellow,
employ the number five,
abolish the laws of the four preceding dynasties,
and thus take up the Mandate of Heaven.
This is an opportunity that comes but once in a thousand years;
it must not be missed.
Gāozǔ admired this but could not put it to use;
the reason for this
is that I may perhaps be engaging in the work of the Duke of Zhōu.
Therefore, which of the ‘Twelve Strategies’ should come first?
One must certainly first set the beginning in order.
Wèi Yǒng, when serving as magistrate of Lóngmén,
upon arrival, enlarged the public offices.
On hearing this, the Master said:
‘This is not what should come first.
Wearing out the people for one’s own ease,
why busy oneself with this?’
Yǒng promptly ceased and apologized to the Master.
The Master said:
‘If one is neither diligent nor frugal,
one cannot be above others.’
Disciples Dòu Wēi, Jiǎ Qióng, and Yáo Yì studied the Lǐ;
Wēn Yànbó, Dù Rúhuì, and Chén Shúdá studied the Yuè;
Dù Yán, Fáng Qiáo, and Wèi Zhēng studied the Shū;
Lǐ Jìng, Xuē Fāngshì, Péi Xī, and Wáng Guī studied the Shī;
Shū Tián studied the Yuánjīng;
Dǒng Cháng, Qiú Zhāng, Xuē Shōu, and Chéng Yuánbèi heard the doctrines of the Six Classics.
Níng Cháng heard:
‘Those who are not specialized in the Classics,
I do not dare to accept as my students.’
The Classics also have various interpretations;
therefore, I have recorded them.
The Master of Tàiyuán Prefecture said:
‘The teaching of Wénzhōngzǐ
cannot remain unannounced.
Days and months pass by;
we must not let the descendants of Wénzhōng fail to hear of it down to this day.’
He summoned his three sons and instructed them in the ‘Summary of Principles’.
The Master of Tàiyuán Prefecture named Níng,
acted with decorum;
he observed a solemn bearing,
and his sons would not appear before him without proper official dress;
within the private chambers, it was as though in the court.
In former times, Wénzhōngzǐ said:
‘Of the worthy,
it is Níng;
but in terms of authority, he is yet lacking,
though he can be entrusted to establish things.’
The Master of the Prefecture bowed twice and said:
‘I respectfully accept your instruction.’
He never acted without propriety throughout his life.
During the Zhēnguān period,
he began his career as Censor of Inspection,
impeaching Hóu Jūnjí for lacking the mind of serving the ruler.
When he retired,
he brought harmony to his town and village.
He governed his family by four teachings:
diligence, frugality, respectfulness, and forbearance;
and regulated his household with four rites:
capping, marriage, mourning, and sacrifice.
Whenever the savings accumulated over three years were sufficient,
he would distribute them among his kin.
The writings of sages and ritual vessels of official dress he never borrowed.
The walls and roofs of his house, and every item within, were sure to be sturdy and simple,
saying: Do not spend carelessly;
the trees and fruit in the courtyard must always be in regular rows,
saying: Do not let things be disorderly.
He served his elder sister-in-law with noted humility and compliance,
never spoke difficultly with others,
and accepted no gifts.
If not by his own strength,
if not his rightful salary,
he never used it for clothing or food.
At meals and banquets, there were never extra dishes,
saying, if according with ritual, it is enough;
at home he did not eat meat,
saying, seeking satiety is not the way;
one cloth quilt was used for twenty years without replacement,
saying, let us not waste the resources of the world.
When someone in his village was falsely accused of taxes,
he paid the dues twice in a single year,
and when holding office took his salary calculated by the day.
After the age of seventy,
his hands never ceased holding the Classics.
Whenever relatives or friends acted without righteousness,
he always corrected them,
saying: To praise in their face but slander behind their backs,
I cannot bear it.
In gatherings and discussions,
he never spoke of others’ faults.
He always maintained a demeanor that could not be transgressed,
and so petty men kept their distance.
Dù Yán said: “Can the Xùjīng be put into practice?”
The Master of Tàiyuán Prefecture said:
“For the princes and great men, it is most urgent.
The Way of the Former Kings
is all contained herein.
When there is order in the world,
the sage promotes and practices it;
when there is no order,
the sage preserves and conceals it.
What is meant by—when it flows, it becomes a river;
when obstructed, it becomes a deep pool;
when ascending, it becomes a cloud;
when spread, it becomes rain;
when hidden, it moistens;
wherever it goes, how can it not bring benefit?”
The Master of Tàiyuán Prefecture said:
“When the Master gained Chéng, Qiú, Dǒng, and Xuē, the Six Classics became brighter.
The composition of dialogues
was due to the strength of these four men.
Dǒng and Qiú died early,
and then Chéng and Xuē passed away in succession.
The teaching of Wénzhōngzǐ,
it has not yet been completed.
Alas!
Let us await the sages to come.
The teaching of Wénzhōngzǐ
continues the Way of the Primal Kings;
therefore, The Treatise on the Kingly Way is placed first.
The ancient sage kings
harmonized their virtue with heaven and earth,
and so next is placed The Treatise on Heaven and Earth.
Heaven is honored and earth is lowly,
ruler and minister are thus established;
so next is The Treatise on Serving the Lord.
To serve the ruler in the model of heaven
is embodied best by the Duke of Zhōu,
so next is The Treatise on the Duke of Zhōu.
The Way of the Duke of Zhōu
is most mysterious in the Yì,
so next is The Treatise on Inquiring into the Yì.
The Yì
is the source of transformation in teaching;
nothing surpasses ritual and music in transformation,
so next is The Treatise on Rites and Music.
When rites and music are widely practiced and illustrious, comes history,
so next is The Treatise on Interpreting History.
In flourishing culture and establishing institutions,
harmonizing regulations is paramount,
and only Wèi Xiàng achieved this,
so next is The Treatise on Wèi Xiàng.
When yin and yang are harmonized,
then nature and principle are understood.
To exhaust principle and fulfill nature to reach destiny,
so next is The Treatise on Establishing Destiny.
Those who comprehend the theories of nature and destiny,
without the Yì, how could they attain this?
The Guān family,
were profound in the Yì,
so next is The Treatise on Guān Lǎng, which concludes the work.”
Wénzhōngzǐ,
of the Wáng clan,
given name Tōng,
courtesy name Zhòngyān.
His ancestor in times past was Bà, who held the title of Hàn Zhēngjūn,
who maintained his purity and did not serve in office.
His eighteenth-generation ancestor was Yīn,
Governor of Yúnzhōng,
whose family resided in Qí,
instructing the local people with the Chunqiu and Zhou Yi,
thus providing for his descendants.
His fourteenth-generation ancestor was Shù,
who ably propagated the achievements of his predecessors,
and composed the *Chunqiu Yìtǒng*,
but declined summons from official bureaus.
His ninth-generation ancestor was Yù,
who suffered the calamities of Mǐn and Huái,
and so moved eastward thereafter.
Yù begot Hǎn,
Hǎn begot Xiù,
both of whom became renowned for their literary scholarship.
Xiù had two sons,
the elder being called Xuánmó,
the younger Xuánzé;
Xuánmó advanced by military strategy,
Xuánzé rose through Confucian learning.
Xuánzé's courtesy name was Yànfǎ,
who was the sixth-generation ancestor of Wénzhōngzǐ.
He served the Song,
and held offices as Táipǔ and Guózǐ Bóshì;
he often sighed and said:
“What my forebears valued was rites and music;
those who had not studied took up soldiery.
What has my elder brother done?
” Thereupon, he devoted himself to the pursuit of morality and virtue,
examined the classics and texts,
and said that accomplishment could not be achieved in small ways,
thus he ultimately became a grand Confucian scholar;
he believed that high office should not be held carelessly,
so in the end he served as a Bóshì,
saying that this was the occupation of the Master,
and it should not be neglected.
The Master,
having received his teachings, called them “Mr. Wáng's tradition.”
Thus his reputation was greatly esteemed among Confucians,
and his descendants continued that excellence for generations.
The Master begot Jiāngzhōu Fǔjūn Huàn,
and Huàn begot Qiú.
Qiú was the first to serve in the north under Wèi,
and during the Tàihé era was Inspector of Bìngzhōu,
his family settled at Héfén,
and he was called Jìnyáng Mùgōng.
Mùgōng begot Yàn, who was Inspector of Tóngzhōu,
and was known as Tóngzhōu Fǔjūn.
Yàn begot the Inspector of Jìzhōu,
known also as Ānkāng Xiàn Gōng.
Ānkāng Xiàn Gōng begot Tóngchuān Fǔjūn,
given name Lóng,
courtesy name Bógāo,
who was the father of Wénzhōngzǐ,
and transmitted the teachings of his master,
instructing more than a thousand disciples.
At the beginning of the Kāihuáng era of the Suí,
he served as Guózǐ Bóshì and awaited imperial summons at Yúnlóng Gate.
At that time, the state had newly settled matters of abdication,
and was establishing the realm through reverence and frugality.
The Emperor, in conversation, asked Fǔjūn:
“What kind of ruler am I?”
Fǔjūn replied:
“Your Majesty is sagacious and divinely martial,
having attained it from Heaven,
issuing decrees and commands,
but not entirely adhering to antiquity.
Though possessing the virtues of Yáo and Shùn,
in the end a lack of learning becomes a hindrance.”
The Emperor was silent, then said:
“You, Master, are my Lù Jiǎ.
With what will you instruct me?”
Fǔjūn, in response to the imperial command, composed seven chapters of the *On the Essentials of Rise and Fall*.
Whenever he presented them,
the Emperor praised them,
yet did not deeply comprehend them.
Fǔjūn then served as Magistrate of Chánglè,
later transferred to Yīshì and Tóngchuān,
and his governance in those places was highly esteemed,
but when his term ended, he retired and returned home,
never serving in office again.
In the fourth year of Kāihuáng,
Wénzhōngzǐ was born.
Tóngchuān Fǔjūn divined for him,
received the “Kūn” changing to “Shī” hexagram,
and presented the omen to Ānkāng Xiàn Gōng.
Xiàn Gōng said:
“This is the hexagram of the Pure King—why has it come?
Two of Earth transform into one of Heaven;
superior virtue occupying a lowly position,
able to rectify the multitude;
such one may rule as king.
Though possessing the virtue of a sovereign,
is it not the proper time?
This child will surely be able to comprehend the aspirations of the world.”
Thus, he was named “Tōng.”
In the ninth year of Kāihuáng,
Jiāngdōng was pacified.
Tóngchuān Fǔjūn sighed and said:
“The kingly Way is without order;
how can the world be unified?”
Wénzhōngzǐ was then ten years old, attending at his side,
and, with a sorrowful countenance, said:
“I have heard
that in ancient times, when ruling a state,
rulers had plans for long-lasting rule,
thus between Xià and Yīn, for several centuries,
all within the Four Seas was ever unified.
But later rulers,
practiced expedient policies,
so that from Wèi and Jìn onward, for hundreds of years,
no stable lord ruled the Nine Provinces.
Above, the Way was lost,
and the people have long been scattered.
Now unity, now division—
what constancy is there?
The Master's sighs
must be due to worry that the imperial order is enfeebled,
and disorder is coming below?”
