Tóngchuān Fǔjūn was impressed and said:
“Is it indeed so?”
Whereupon he told him of the matter of the Yuánjīng,
and Wénzhōngzǐ bowed twice to receive it.
In his eighteenth year,
Tóngchuān Fǔjūn was at home in leisure,
sang the “Fámù,”
and summoned Wénzhōngzǐ.
Wénzhōngzǐ, startled, bowed twice and said:
“May I ask, Master, what is your aim?”
Tóngchuān Fǔjūn said:
“Come here!
From the Son of Heaven down to the commoners,
none have succeeded without the aid of friends.
Among the three relationships,
the teacher is foremost.
Since the Way was lost,
this has long been forsaken,
and so what constancy is there?
My child, strive diligently,
soar before you alight.”
From then on, Wénzhōngzǐ aspired to travel the four quarters.
In truth, he studied the *Shū* with Dōnghǎi Lǐ Yù,
the *Shī* with Huìjī Xià Tián,
questioned about ritual with Hédōng Guān Zǐmíng,
corrected music with Běipíng Huò Jí,
and investigated the *Yì* with his kinsman Zhònghuá.
He did not take off his clothes (to rest) for six years;
such was his concentrated will.
In the third year of Rénshòu,
Wénzhōngzǐ crossed the capping ceremony,
and was deeply moved with a desire to succor the common people.
He traveled west to Cháng’ān,
and met Emperor Wéndì of Suí.
The Emperor sat in the Hall of Supreme Polarity to summon him,
whereupon he presented twelve “Strategies for Great Peace,”
strategies to honor the kingly Way,
to promote the arts of hegemony,
and to examine the present and verify by the past.
How grandly did he move the world as if it were held in the palm of his hand.
The Dì was greatly pleased and said,
“It was almost too late for me to obtain Shēng.
Heaven granted Shēng to me as a gift.”
He sent down the matter for discussion among the gōng and qīng.
The gōng and qīng were displeased.
At that time, there was about to be strife within palace walls.
Wénzhōngzǐ knew that his plans would not be employed.
He composed the “Song of the Eastern Expedition” and withdrew, saying,
“I think of my country,
traveling far to the capital precincts.
Suddenly I encounter the sovereign,
who bestows courtesy upon a man in plain garments.
Thus I cherish the heart of the ancients,
and wish to lay the foundation for great peace.
The times are strange and affairs changing,
my aspirations are thwarted, my wishes denied.
Alas!
The Way is not carried out,
and I let my wings droop, returning east.
The Sovereign never decides,
and I weary my body, flying west.”
The Dì, hearing this, summoned him again,
but he did not come.
In the fourth year,
the Dì passed away.
In the first year of Dàyè,
he was summoned once more but did not come,
declining on account of illness.
He said to those close to him,
“I am a man of Zhōu,
my family hails from Qí.
During the chaos of Yǒngjiā,
we migrated east,
and Mù Gōng, the great ancestor, first served Wèi.
At the time between Wèi and Zhōu,
we rendered great service to the people,
and the Son of Heaven bestowed land on us.
We first settled at Hé Fén,
and thus our ancestral tombs have been here for four generations.
This land,
its people are deeply anxious and thoughtful,
preserving the lingering airs of the Táotáng clan,
as cherished by the ancestors.
There is my humble hut beneath a thatched eave,
with earth steps like little heaps.
Since the Way is not practiced,
how can one find peace here?
I will simply withdraw my resolve and keep to the Way.”
Thus he continued the Shī and the Shū,
rectified the Lǐ and the Yuè,
amended the Yuánjīng,
praised the Dào of the Yì,
and after nine years greatly accomplished the Six Classics.
Disciples came from afar.
Dǒng Cháng of Hénán,
Yáo Yì of Tàishān,
Dù Yán of Jīngzhào,
Lǐ Jìng of Zhàojùn,
Chéng Yuán of Nányáng,
Dòu Wēi of Fūfēng,
Xuē Shōu of Hédōng,
Jiǎ Qióng of Zhōngshān,
Fáng Xuánlíng of Qīnghé,
Wèi Zhēng of Jùlù,
Wēn Dàyǎ of Tàiyuán,
Chén Shūdá of Yǐngchuān, and others,
all faced north to acknowledge him as master,
receiving the Way of assisting the king.
As for those coming and going to receive teaching,
they were beyond counting,
probably more than a thousand.
At the end of Suí,
the teaching of Wénzhōngzǐ flourished in Hé Fén,
dignified and harmonious.
In the tenth year of Dàyè,
the Shàngshū summoned him to be Registrar of Shǔ Prefecture,
but he did not accept.
In the eleventh year, summoned as Assistant Literary Gentleman and National Academician,
he likewise did not go.
In the thirteenth year,
disorder arose at Jiāngdū.
The master's son was ill,
and he summoned Xuē Shōu,
saying,
“I dreamed that Yán Huí received Kǒngzǐ’s command, saying:
‘Return and rest,
it is surely the Master who calls me.
Why wish for long life?’
I will not recover.
And so he passed away.
Several hundred disciples gathered to discuss:
‘Is it not that our master was truly one who has attained to the utmost?
From Zhòngní till now,
none such has appeared.
The Lǐ says,
‘When a man is born, he is given a courtesy name,
to display his virtue;
when he dies, he receives a posthumous name,
to change his name.
The Master was born in a time of chaos,
and none paid him homage,
so he continued the Shī and the Shū,
rectified the Lǐ and the Yuè,
amended the Yuánjīng,
praised the Way of the Yì,
realizing the grand aim of the Sage,
and accomplished all that could be done under Heaven.
Since the passing of Zhòngní,
has not civilization rested here?
The Yì says,
“The yellow robe is supremely auspicious,
for the pattern lies within.”
Let us petition to name him Wénzhōngzǐ.’
They set silks and hempen garment at his place,
and mourned to send him off.
When the rites were complete,
they returned all the writings of Wénzhōngzǐ to the Wáng clan.
“Treatise on Rites,” twenty-five chapters,
arranged into ten juàn.
“Treatise on Music,” twenty chapters,
arranged into ten juàn.
“Continued Shū,” one hundred fifty chapters,
arranged into twenty-five juàn.
“Continued Shī,” three hundred sixty chapters,
arranged into ten juàn.
“Yuánjīng,” fifty chapters,
arranged into fifteen juàn.
“Praise of the Yì,” seventy chapters,
arranged into ten juàn.
All were not yet published.
Meeting an age of loss and chaos,
the late gentlewoman hid the books in a chest,
carrying them everywhere,
never leaving them.
In the fourth year of Wǔdé of the Táng,
order was restored.
The late gentlewoman returned to the old home,
and then handed the books to her younger brother Níng.
Wénzhōngzǐ had two sons:
the elder was Fújiāo,
the younger was Fúzhì.
In the year of the Dragon’s Ascent under the Great Táng,
the realm flourished in prosperity,
but the teachings of Wénzhōngzǐ were not yet widespread,
and among the younger gentlemen, few could know them.
During Zhēnguàn,
Wèi Wéngōng was ill,
and Elder Uncle, Lord of Tàiyuán, paid him a visit,
staying overnight, conversing at a banquet,
and sighing in the middle of the night.
The Lord of Tàiyuán said,
‘Why do you sigh?’
Wèi Gōng said,
‘In the time of Dàyè,
I once served with various worthies at the side of Wénzhōngzǐ,
and he said to me, Wéi, and to Fáng, Dù, and others:
“Though you seniors are brilliant and distinguished,
yet you are not equal to Dǒng, Xuē, Chéng, and Qiú.
Even if you meet an enlightened sovereign, you will still be ashamed in matters of rites and music.”
At that time, I was displeased,
but Wénzhōngzǐ laughed and said,
“In time, when you face affairs,
you will come to understand yourself.”
At the beginning of Zhēnguàn,
all those worthies had passed away,
but I, Fáng, Lǐ, Wēn, and Dù were able to ascend to prominence,
and in every great matter of state, never failed to participate.
The assembled ministers said:
“From the time I resided in the princely residence,
up to attaining the supreme throne,
you, my ministers, have always admonished me with serious faces.
All of you claimed:
‘Worthy words and good strategies,
the trouble is that the ruler does not enact them;
if they were enacted,
then even the Three Sovereigns would not suffice to make a fourth,
nor the Five Emperors to make a sixth.’
I am indeed humble and unworthy,
yet my judgments have always been cautious.
Although my virtue does not rival Qí,
nor does my wisdom approach that of Jùnzhé,
yet when I hear righteousness, I submit to it;
in this, I am perhaps not far from the ancients.
If any of you have plans for enduring governance,
present them one by one;
let there be no concealment.
” Fáng, Dù and others received the imperial order, dancing for joy,
and praised the Emperor’s virtue.
The Emperor said:
“Enough.
” He led the assembled ministers to feast inside.
When the wine was being circulated,
the Emperor said:
“In establishing laws and implementing transformation,
the highest value lies in lasting endurance.
From Qín and Hàn onwards,
there is nothing there worthy of imitation.
Of the losses and gains of the Three Dynasties,
which is appropriate to follow?
Answer me with all your hearts,
and do not worry your advice will not be enacted.
” At that time none of the ministers dared to answer,
Zhēng sat below,
signaled to by Fáng and Dù,
who caused him to move forward and reply:
“The rites of Xià and Yīn cannot be precisely ascertained,
and the transforming power of loyalty and respect
is something we have only heard described.
Confucius said:
‘In the Zhōu, he had the example of the two previous dynasties;
how majestic and accomplished was its culture!
I follow Zhōu.’
The *Zhōulǐ*,
edited by Gōng Dàn;
the *Shī* and *Shū*,
compiled by Zhòngní;
though the rules and discipline have decayed and been lost,
yet the standards and systems are all there.
Xún and Mèng expounded them before us,
Dǒng and Jiǎ expanded them afterwards,
their remaining words and transmitted meanings
can be fully adopted and enacted.
If Your Majesty seeks to reconstruct the grand tombs and
remake the regulations of emperors,
then this exceeds what the mediocre and weak can discuss.
But if you select the regulations of previous ages,
and illuminate the kingly way,
then I ask that the *Zhōudiǎn* be always put into effect.”
The Emperor was greatly pleased.
The next day,
he again summoned Fáng, Dù, and Zhēng together to enter,
and said:
“Last night I read the *Zhōulǐ*;
truly a work created by a sage.
Its opening words say:
‘When the king establishes the state,
he clarifies the regions and sets the proper positions,
organizes the state and plans the fields,
appoints officials and divides offices,
to make them the utmost model for the people.’
How true and profound this is!
” After a long while, he said to Zhēng:
“I have pondered this;
if we do not have the well-field system, do not have feudal enfeoffment, do not use corporal punishments, and yet wish to carry out the way of the Duke of Zhōu,
it cannot be achieved.
The great meaning of the *Yìjīng*
is to follow the times and suit the people.
Zhōu Rèn once said:
‘Offer your abilities, then take your place.’
If it were possible to enact them all, one by one,
truly this is my wish.
But if it cannot be fully attained,
and we strive forcefully to follow the great way,
yet fail to achieve the ideal,
we would, in painting a tiger and failing,
become the object of laughter for posterity.
You all must consider this fully.”
He thus commanded them to stay in the Central Secretariat,
where they deliberated for several days,
but could not reach a decision,
and so Zhēng soon requested to withdraw.
Although the Emperor did not raise the matter again,
on another occasion at a quiet banquet, he said to Zhēng:
“Rites have decayed, and music has collapsed;
I deeply feel compassion for this.
Formerly, Emperor Zhāng of Hàn cherished Zhāng Chún,
and now I urgently value you all the same.
To have an aspiration and not achieve it—
this is what the ancients sorrowed over.”
Zhēng knelt and replied:
“No one but Your Majesty could carry this out.
Because we, your ministers, had no established achievements beforehand,
what shame would there be in that?
Yet Emperor Wén of Hàn enriched the state by ruling with clarity and calmness,
and Emperor Xiào Xuān practiced discipline and perfected the reality behind names,
Emperor Guāngwǔ assigned responsibility to his officials,
so that his meritorious ministers remained intact,
and Emperor Sùzōng emphasized learning and respected teachers,
the Confucian spirit flourished greatly.
Your Majesty’s virtue is uniquely eminent,
embodying all those qualities.
Though you may not yet surpass the Three Dynasties,
yet you are a rarity in a thousand years.
It is for Your Majesty to be ever vigilant though already illustrious;
as for the rules and numbers of ritual and music,
give them thoughtful consideration in due time;
as for the working of teaching and transformation,
why worry if it comes late?”
The Emperor said:
“Opportunities are hard to obtain and easy to lose;
that is why I am so anxious.
You may withdraw,
let there be no more discussion.”
Zhēng, together with Fáng, Dù, and others, were all abashed and fearful,
and after two bows, departed.
Fáng said to Zhēng:
“Xuánlíng and you devote your utmost strength to assisting the state;
yet when it comes to the discussion of rituals and music,
unless one is a great talent destined for the age,
he cannot fully meet the clarity of Your Majesty’s light.”
In former days, Wénzhōngzǐ did not treat the teaching of ritual and music as gifts for me,
and there was good reason for this.
If Dǒng and Xuē were here,
perhaps we would not have come to this end. Alas!
If there is a head but no arms and legs,
how can one not lament such a state?”
In the seventeenth year,
Duke Wèi passed away,
and the Lord of Tàiyuán Prefecture mourned him deeply.
In the nineteenth year,
he bestowed on me the *Zhōng Shuō*,
and also recounted to me the words of Duke Wèi,
thus narrating these events.
It was the twentieth year of Zhēnguàn,
the ninth month when this was recorded.
The Master of East Ridge,
named Jì,
styled Wúgōng,
was the youngest brother of Wénzhōngzǐ.
He abandoned office and did not serve,
farming at East Ridge,
calling himself the East Ridge Master.
At the beginning of Zhēnguàn,
my second uncle, the Honorable Lord of Tàiyuán Prefecture, was Censorate Inspector,
impeached Hóu Jūnjí,
and thereby implicated Chancellor Chángsūn,
for which he was found guilty.
At that time Dù Yán was Grand Censor,
and secretly memorialized that my second uncle had spoken frankly
and was not at fault.
From this, enmity arose between the Chancellor and Lord Dù,
and all the Wang brothers were suppressed and unused.
My youngest uncle was on good terms with Minister Chén Shùdá.
Compiled it.
Duke Chén also avoided the power of the Tàiwèi,
hiding away and not appearing,
repeatedly sending letters to Jìfù,
speaking earnestly and with sincerity.
Jìfù replied with a letter.
The gist of it says:
“My deceased elder brother once traveled with various gentlemen,
discoursing on the way of emperors and kings,
most thoroughly.
I and our second brother waited by his side,
and heard much of the great principles.
The late elder brother said:
‘We are descendants of the Zhōu,
our family has practiced rites and music for generations.
When our descendants encounter a true king and can promote these teachings,
then the Confucian legacy will not perish—
could it be Heaven’s will?
Could it be Heaven’s will?’
At that time, Wèi Wén Gōng responded:
‘Sir, you have successors.
Heaven will make it manifest.
If Zhēng ever encounters an enlightened sovereign,
I wish to support this Way,
not daring ever to forget it.’
Later, when our second brother was appointed magistrate of Húsū,
Dù Dàfū once spoke frankly before the court of his honesty and loyalty.
The Tàiwèi heard and grew angry,
while Wèi Gōng happened to enter to present affairs,
and saw the Tàiwèi.
Wèi Gōng said:
‘Was the matter regarding Jūnjí truly baseless?
Did the Censor reverse his judgment rightly?
Why does the Tàiwèi doubt?’
Thereupon, his anger began to subside.
Yet Dù and my second brother maintained their resolve, unyielding,
and Wèi Gōng also withdrew from court in silence.
Afterwards, Jūnjí was indeed executed.
But can it be that my family is always unfortunate, suffering persecution for plain speaking?
Or is this a way of opening the Way?
I have now been farming in the fields for years,
without a single word to benefit the present age,
without a single position to leave my mark.
I will end my days in the eastern hills,
content only in alternately drunken and sober ease.
Yet I remember the literary works of our late and learned forebear,
and among the disciples who have received instruction, half have risen to positions in court and temple.
The ‘Continued Canons’ and the ‘Central Discourses’ have not yet been taught and spread.
Alas!
Since you know my heart, what else do you seek from me?
Remember the words of my late elder brother,
and perhaps they will not perish;
that is enough.
I respectfully record this after compiling the ‘Lineage Accounts’,
now I am at Fújiāo,
where I fully understood his intentions face to face.
What a blessing,
what a blessing!
Guān Lǎng, styled Zǐmíng,
was a native of Jiè in Hédōng.
He possessed great talent for statecraft,
and was supremely skilled in divination and calculation.
Floating and sinking within his hometown,
he did not seek office or fame.
At the end of Tàihé,
my fifth-generation ancestor Mù Gōng was enfeoffed at Jìnyáng,
and in the Secretariat appointed Lǎng as registrar to the ducal residence.
Mù Gōng discussed the ‘Yì’ with him,
and both admired each other's insight.
Mù Gōng said to him:
‘You have unusual talent,
you must not let the Son of Heaven fail to recognize you.’
He went in to report to Emperor Xiàowén,
saying:
‘Zhāng Yí and Guō Zuò have spoken of him,
but I took divination and calculation as petty skills,
and did not grant him audience.’
Mù Gōng replied:
‘This man’s understanding of patterns of the Way and subtle words is deep,
perhaps even Zhāng Yí and Guō Zuò cannot fully comprehend it.’
He was summoned to an audience,
and the Emperor questioned him about the ‘Lǎozi’ and the ‘Yìjīng’,
and Lǎng gave profound explanations on mysterious teachings,
truly discussing the royal Way,
urging the Emperor to make benevolence and frugality his foundation,
adorned with law, administration, rites, and music.
The Emperor praised him,
and said to Mù Gōng:
‘Sir, you know men well.
Yesterday I saw Zǐmíng,
and his talent is like Guǎn Zhòng or Yuè Yì!
How could this be mere skill in calculation?’
Mù Gōng bowed twice in reply, saying:
‘In former days Yī Yǐn carried the cauldron and assisted Chéng Tāng,
now Zǐmíng uses calculation to approach Your Majesty.
The meeting of ruler and minister always springs from some cause.
Hereafter, he should be entrusted with office.’
The Emperor said:
‘For now, discuss divination with him together.’
Soon after, he was frequently granted audiences for several days,
returning only at dusk.
There was an expedition against the Wūhuán,
and Zǐmíng was ordered to go with Mù Gōng to garrison Bìngzhōu,
with all important military and state affairs reported by urgent courier,
thus it was that Mù Gōng used the ‘Yì’ to divine,
always with results like a spirit’s.
Earlier, when Mù Gōng was in Jiāngzuǒ,
he was displeased with the death of Yuán Càn,
and shamed to eat Qí grain,
so after the Xiāo clan usurped the throne, Mù Gōng fled north,
which was in the first year of Qí Jiànyuán,
and the third year of Wèi Tàihé.
At that time, Mù Gōng was already fifty-two.
When reporting affairs, he said:
‘In the fourth year of Dà’ān,
this humble official was born.’
This was the second year of Sòng Dàmíng.
On coming north and traveling through Hédōng,
no one recognized him,
only Lúyáng Wū Shēn marveled at him and said:
‘He is a minister of royal caliber.’
In the eighth year of Tàihé,
he was summoned as Secretary in the Secretariat,
and promoted to Censorate Yellow Gate Attendant Gentleman.
It was believed that Emperor Xiàowén harbored the intention to restore order to the world,
but the institutions were not yet established;
so in leisurely gatherings,
he frequently memorialized and made proposals,
which the Emperor humbly received.
When the capital moved to Luòyì,
and Wáng Xiāo was advanced,
it was due to Mù Gōng's secret strategies.
He also recommended Guān Zǐmíng,
whom the Emperor also respected and admired,
saying to Mù Gōng:
‘Excellent plans and far-sighted strategies—
do not worry they will not be used.
When I return from southern campaign,
we shall together discuss the Way,
to fully grasp the principles of governance.’
Mù Gōng and Lǎng joyfully congratulated each other, saying:
‘Such an opportunity comes but once in a thousand years!’
But soon the Emperor died,
and Mù Gōng returned to Luòyì,
and within a year passed away,
after which Lǎng never served in office again.
The Governor of Tóngzhōu studied under him,
learning the ‘Chūnqiū’ and the ‘Yìjīng’,
and together they lived in seclusion on Línfén Mountain.
In the fourth year of Jǐngmíng,
after the Governor of Tóngzhōu had completed mourning, he took up the qín,
playing with deep feeling and thoughts of the troubled times.
When Zǐmíng heard it, he said:
‘How sorrowful are these sounds!’
The Governor replied:
I grieve that the former lord and Xiānshēng had aspirations that were not fulfilled.
Zǐmíng said:
“If there is joy, then act on it;
if there is sorrow, then avoid it.”
The Prefect said:
“Yàn has heard that
in matters of order and chaos, of loss and gain,
each arises repeatedly according to certain cycles.
If one can deduce its course,
the affairs of a hundred generations can be known.
I wish that Xiānshēng would perform a divination to decide the matter;
what do you think?”
Zǐmíng said:
“Divination and calculation are subtle and obscure;
if one divines often, it breeds confusion.
Permit me to consult the milfoil stalks
and use the hexagram to judge by centuries.”
The Prefect said:
“Agreed.”
Thereupon, the milfoil stalks were manipulated and the hexagram cast,
yielding Guài changing to Gé (Duì above Qián below) (Duì above Lí below).
He set aside the milfoil and sighed, saying:
“Now, the great cycle
will not last beyond two further transmissions.
From the upcoming Jiǎshēn year,
after twenty-four years to Wùshēn,
a great turmoil and calamity will begin.
In the palace, there will be a foreign minister wielding power,
and the generations will submit to his strength.
If he is employed according to the Way,
it will be like the actions of Huán and Wén;
if not by the Way,
then ruler and minister alike will be slaughtered.
” The Prefect said:
“From where will this person arise?”
Lǎng said:
“On the ruins of Sandài,
there is a peculiar aura;
if it is to appear,
would it not be on the outskirts of Bìng?”
The Prefect said:
“If this person cannot rise,
to whom will all living beings turn?”
He said:
“There will be two heroes rising, and the Central Plain will be divided.”
The Prefect said:
“Can each of them succeed?”
Lǎng said:
“When there is an opening, they move—
how could they not succeed?
Even if worthy men support them,
I am afraid they will not succeed.
” The Prefect said:
“Please specify the years.”
Lǎng said:
“It will begin in Jiǎyín
and end in Gēngzǐ—
this is the number of Heaven.”
The Prefect said:
“Which state will perish first?”
Lǎng said:
“If one does not fight with virtue but uses deceit and cunning,
then the old regime will fall first.”
The Prefect said:
“What about afterwards?”
Lǎng said:
“In the Xīnchǒu year,
there will be a ruler who is reverent and frugal,
rising from among commoners to unite the world.”
The Prefect said:
“Is it in the southeast?”
Lǎng said:
“It must be in the northwest.
One cannot pacify great chaos by civil governance alone;
martial might is required.
Moreover, the northwest is a land of martial strength.
In the southeast,
their customs become rapacious;
in the northwest,
their rise is vigorous.
Furthermore, as for the southeast,
it was the former master of Zhōngguó;
but the authority of Zhōngguó has long lain in ruin.
What Heaven has cast down,
who can revive?”
The Prefect said:
“Can one fix the years of the southeast?”
Lǎng said:
“The fate of the southeast
will not exceed three centuries.
Great worthies and great sages
are seldom encountered,
so if it can complete its era,
it would be most fortunate.
And in the Xīnchǒu year,
a luminous ruler will arise,
and the one who pacifies the world will do so within no more than nine years.
In Jǐyǒu,
Jiāngdōng will be endangered—is it not so?”
The Prefect said:
“Once the luminous ruler arises,
how will his rule be?”
He replied:
“It has a beginning and an end;
the transformation of the Five Emperors and the Three Kings will be restored.
If not established by the Way,
then it will end in arrogance and excess,
and in its late years and final decline,
there will be tyrants like Jié and Zhòu.
The Way of the Former Kings has been cast aside for so long;
harsh changes and cruel governance
will ultimately reach severe extremity.
Therefore it is said:
After a great army,
must come years of calamity;
after accumulated chaos,
must come a cruel ruler.
Such is the natural order.”
The Prefect said:
“Will the Way of the Former Kings truly be lost?”
Lǎng said:
“What do you mean, ‘lost’?
When there is long absence of a luminous ruler,
inevitably accomplished men will be born.
They will enact the rites and laws;
this is what connects Heaven, Earth, and mankind, and the Five Constant Virtues.
As Kǒngzǐ said:
‘When King Wén passed away,
did not culture remain here?’
Therefore, the royal Way cannot be lost.”
The Prefect said:
“Pray, deduce its numbers.”
Lǎng said:
“The strategies of Qián and Kūn,
the calculations of yīn and yáng,
when pursued, do not exceed three hundred and sixty-six;
when extended and prolonged, do not exceed three hundred and eighty-four;
this is the Way of Heaven. Ah!
Lǎng has heard that
the Former Sages and the images of the hexagrams correspond.
From Wèi onward,
there has been no true lord in all-under-Heaven.
Thus from the first year of Huángchū, in Gēngzǐ,
until now is eighty-four years;
after another eighty-two years to Bǐngwǔ,
it will be a total of three hundred and sixty-six,
and then the accomplished will arise.
After another eighteen years to Jiǎzǐ,
will he not align with the kingly one?
If used, kingly Way will be revived;
if not,
the teachings of Zhū and Sì will be cultivated.
” The Prefect said:
“Where will this person arise?”
Lǎng said:
“Perhaps on the borders of Táng and Jìn.
In ancient times, after the end of the Yīn, rulership did not return, and Zhòngní was born in Zhōu;
when rulership did not return to Zhōu,
then such a man would arise in Jìn.
Those born in Zhōu
inherited the remaining virtue of the Duke of Zhōu;
those born in Jìn
inherited the remnant customs of Táotáng.
Heaven and Earth are mysteriously linked;
their numbers follow nature.”
The Prefect said:
“What shall come afterwards?”
Lǎng said:
“From Jiǎshēn to Jiǎzǐ
is precisely a hundred years.
Beyond that, none can know.”
The Prefect said:
“Xiānshēng, in explaining the hexagrams,
always holds to two possibilities.”
Lǎng said:
“What do you mean?”
The Prefect said:
“Whenever Xiānshēng speaks of the rise and fall,
you always say, ‘If used according to the Way, aided by worthies, its measure cannot be fathomed’—
is this not two alternatives?”
Lǎng said:
“The images that arise have fixed numbers;
fortune and misfortune have prior signs;
if one can adapt to changes,
then order and chaos can be altered.
Thus, for the noble man, with regard to the Yì,
he observes change and weighs omens when he acts;
he inquires before proceeding,
he examines before making a move.
Advancing at the proper time,
and retreating upon knowing difficulties,
such is why divination and computation were held in high regard by the former kings.
Thus it is said:
the perilous is made safe,
the easy is made praiseworthy,
good people are few and evil people are many,
there are many dark rulers and few enlightened sovereigns.
Yáo and Shùn succeeded to the abdicated throne,
yet such did not occur through all the successive ages;
Yī and Zhōu restored order,
but even near antiquity saw this come to an end.
Is it that the Mandate cannot be changed,
or that transformation cannot be carried out?
The Way is abiding, but human generations are fleeting;
thus the search for talent is indeed difficult.
Sometimes there are ministers without a ruler,
sometimes there are rulers without ministers,
thus those who preserve both are few indeed.
Zhòngní said:
"If only someone would employ me,
would I not bring about an Eastern Zhōu?"
This is a case of ministers without a ruler.
Emperor Zhāng said:
"When Yáo composed the Dàzhāng,
one Kuí alone was sufficient."
This is a case of a ruler without ministers.
Thus, the achievements of Wén and Wǔ
ultimately fell into the hands of Zhòngní;
the excellence of ritual and music
was not realized in the time of Emperor Zhāng.
The gradual causes of order and chaos must have their root,
yet the completion of prosperity and downfall is rarely encountered to the end.
The Yìjīng says:
"Achievements and undertakings are manifested in change."
This is what is meant.
Why say there are not two alternatives!
"The Prefect said:
"The Duke of Zhōu established the tripods in Jiá and Rǔ,
divining the generations to be thirty,
divining the years to be eight hundred;
was this, too, two alternatives?"
Lǎng replied:
"Sages assist and harmonize Heaven and Earth,
Yīn and Yáng,
expand and uphold the magnificent order,
establish the utmost standard for mankind,
compile strategies to steer events afar,
lay out nets and distant restraints,
make manifest order and disorder before they arise,
calculate success and failure when there are yet no signs.
Surely, there are numbers that do not change,
but periods that are unfixed.
Suppose mediocre rulers maintain it,
or treacherous ministers transgress it,
in the end they cannot hasten the ordained period,
nor disrupt the cycle that has not yet declined.
Thus it is said:
even though the virtue of Zhōu declined,
the Mandate of Heaven was not changed.
The sage knows that enlightened kings and worthy ministers cannot always be encountered,
and that wise plans and sagacious strategies sometimes have their limits.
Therefore, they examine the canons and rites,
consult tortoise and yarrow,
affirm the Mandate of Heaven through human affairs,
and represent the future with calendrical cycles.
Sometimes what has flourished yet declines again,
sometimes the predicted span is not fully attained.
This, then, is the value of sages' methods.
If enlightened kings had succeeded one another,
and able assistants had followed in their footsteps,
then they would surely endure together with Heaven for innumerable years,
how could it be merely thirty generations and eight hundred years?
If the state outlived its predicted span,
it was either by the merit of former kings
or the strength of Huán and Wén.
Heaven’s intent and human affairs,
how could they be in vain?
" The Prefect said:
"Do not tortoise and yarrow proceed from sage counsels?"
Lǎng replied:
"Sage strategy establishes the foundation for what is to come,
tortoise and yarrow reveal events yet to happen;
they complement and confirm each other,
how could there be any difference or contradiction?"
The Prefect said:
"Great indeed is the counsel of humanity!"
Lǎng replied:
"It is human counsel that secures the world in peace.
Now, the world is a vast vessel:
when set on stable ground, it is secure;
when set on perilous ground, it is endangered.
Thus, on a level road, a carriage is safe;
even a madman knows it is hard to overturn.
But riding wild and controlling a rotten vehicle,
even a child knows it must be dangerous.
How could it be that, with the ordinances of the Zhōu rites in effect,
the calendar did not last eight hundred years;
or with the Qín laws established,
the ancestral line could not extend beyond two generations? Alas!
Heaven’s Mandate and human affairs,
do they truly arrive at the same end?"
The Prefect said:
"What, then, is the principle by which you, sir, have set forth the rise and fall of order and chaos?"
Lǎng replied:
"Refinement and plainness are alternately used,
power and fortune ride upon each other.
Examine deficiency and excess to verify the times—
in a hundred generations, nothing is hidden.
Study tortoise and yarrow to assess their deliberations—
and a thousand years can be known.
Have you never thought upon this?
How could there be any remoteness in such matters?"
The Prefect rose in astonishment,
then wrote and stored away these records,
and retired to study the Yìjīng.
It was the Yìjīng doctrine of the Wáng clan
that took Lǎng as its ancestor.
Thereafter,
in the first year of Xuānwǔ’s Zhèngshǐ era, when the year’s stem was Jiǎshēn,
to the first year of Xiàowén’s Yǒngān era, the twenty-fourth year, being Wùshēn,
the Hú Empress caused disorder,
Ěrzhū Róng rose in Bìngzhōu,
ruler and minister destroyed each other,
and slaughter succeeded slaughter.
Zhōu and Qí divided and contended for power,
but were finally united in the West;
this began in Jiǎyín,
and ended in Gēngzǐ,
all just as he had said.
The following year, Xīnchǒu,
Suí Gāozǔ accepted the abdication,
and indeed settled the world through reverence and frugality.
In the first year of Kāihuáng,
Ānkāng Xiàn Gōng, old in his home,
said to the Prefect of Tóngchuān:
"Guān-shēng is nearly a sage;
his words about the future
seem as if tally and contract have come together."
In the fourth year of Kāihuáng,
the Lady of Tóngchuān crossed a mountain ridge,
set foot upon a great stone, and became pregnant;
soon she gave birth to Wénzhōngzǐ,
two years before the predicted date of Bǐngwǔ.
Xiàn Gōng divined, saying:
"This child is destined to know."
In the sixth year of Kāihuáng, Bǐngwǔ,
Wénzhōngzǐ understood the Book of Documents,
and his fame filled the roads.
In the ninth year, Jǐyǒu,
the South of the Yangtze was pacified,
and the policies of Gāozǔ began to be realized.
In the fourth year of Rénshòu, Jiǎzǐ,
Wénzhōngzǐ was granted audience with Gāozǔ,
but the Way did not prevail,
and the institutions of Daye were worse than those of Jié and Zhòu.
Then Wénzhōngzǐ said:
"It is no longer possible to accomplish anything."
He thus retired to live at Fényáng,
continued the Poetry and Documents,
and discoursed on ritual and music.
When Jiāngdū fell,
Wénzhōng fell ill,
and sighed, saying:
"Heaven is about to inaugurate the fortune of Yáo and Shùn,
yet I shall not encounter it.
Alas!
What the Master has spoken has all proved true.
The Prefect of Tàiyuán,
whose given name was Níng,
styled Shūtián,
was the younger brother of Wén Zhōngzǐ.
At the beginning of the Zhēnguàn era,
when the Way of the Superior Man flourished,
the disciples of my late lord were spread throughout the court and government,
intending to propagate his teachings,
to apply them to royal governance,
and thus sought his writings from Zhòngfù.
Zhòngfù, as the compilation and editing were not yet completed, did not release them,
therefore, for generations, none heard the meanings of the Six Classics.
Zhòngfù took off his plain garments,
and became Censor.
At that time, Chief Censor Dù Yán said to Zhòngfù:
"You are the brother of a sage,
do you have any unusual knowledge?"
Zhòngfù replied:
"Níng, being of the same blood,
once attended when my departed elder brother lectured on the Dao at Hé and Fén,
I also took part in this,
yet apart from the Six Classics, I have heard nothing more."
Yán said:
"Previously, the disciples all remembered and recorded it,
namely, Xuē Shōu and Yáo Yì put it together and named it the *Zhōngshuō*.
This book,
is the finest discourse in the realm,
subtle yet manifest,
detailed yet appropriate,
widely encompassing great principles,
broadly elucidating the source of teaching.
In it are the questions disciples asked the Master,
and the deeds of Wén Zhōngzǐ's conduct,
thus.
Why do you not seek it from their families?"
Zhòngfù said:
"Since the time of chaos and disorder,
I have not had occasion to attend to it."
He then withdrew and sought it,
obtaining over one hundred sheets of the *Zhōngshuō*,
mostly miscellaneous notes, without listed chapters,
the first scroll and preface were decayed and obliterated by borers,
and could not be properly arranged.
It happened that Zhòngfù was demoted to be Magistrate of Húsū,
and he sighed, saying:
"The teachings of Wén Zhōngzǐ must not remain unproclaimed,
days and months speed by,
the years do not wait for me."
He then released his seal and returned home,
made a great study against the Six Classics,
and copied and recorded them.
The "Discourse on Rites" and "Discourse on Music" each lost five chapters,
the "Sequels to the Book of Poetry" and "Sequels to the Book of Documents" both lost their "Minor Prefaces,"
but the "Original Classic" and "Appreciation of the Yì" were wholly preserved,
yielding six hundred sixty-five chapters,
which he engraved into seventy-five scrolls,
divided into six sections,
and titled "The Six Classics of the Wáng Family."
Zhòngfù said to his sons:
"Great indeed is my elder brother's work,
in reference to the emperor's law and imperial Way,
it shines brilliantly,
and as to all things between Heaven and Earth,
there is nothing it does not reach.
Since the Spring and Autumn period,
there has never been such a composition as this."
He also said to the disciples:
"Let it not be that the teachings of Wén Zhōngzǐ fail to reach posterity."
So he gathered his sons and transmitted it to them.
In the sixteenth year of Zhēnguàn,
within a single year,
they learned the meanings of the Six Classics;
in three years,
they comprehended most of the general scope.
Ah!
How can mere youngsters hope to understand it,
and yet have taken note of it.
In the nineteenth year,
Zhòngfù was summoned to serve as Recording Officer in Luòzhōu,
and again entrusted the *Zhōngshuō* to me, saying:
"This is the remaining discourse of my late elder brother."
I bowed twice and said:
"As for the teaching of the *Zhōngshuō*,
it strives for conciseness yet attains profundity,
few in words but great in principle,
is it not comparable to the *Analects of Confucius* in its records?
I, your disciple, will receive it,
and not allow it to be lost or fall into neglect."
I thus classified and arranged it into categories and families,
compiled it into ten sections,
and engraved it into ten scrolls.
As for the names and lineages of the disciples,
I consulted records and documents,
and included these in an External Appendix,
as a supplement to the genealogical sources.
Now, with the Six Classics and the *Zhōngshuō*,
through them may one observe the enterprise of my late lord,
how he established principle and clarified the Way,
set forth models and established instruction,
and know that what Wén Zhōngzǐ accomplished
was truly following Heaven's will.
As the years pass further away,
affairs at court differ,
those who shared these intentions have perished and been lost,
the imperial gate has become far and remote,
the teachings of Wén Zhōngzǐ have been suppressed and not put into practice,
alas, how sad!
They are transmitted in vain to descendants as a family legacy, nothing more.
Written in the first month of the twenty-third year of Zhēnguàn.
